2027-03-07.title: Fifth Sunday of the Great Fast
2027-03-07.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Hagar and the God who sees
Hewers of wood and drawers of water
Rivers of living water and the light of the world
2027-03-07.alt: Season of the Great Fast (Sauma Ramba). The fast has passed its midpoint; the fifth week begins.
2027-03-07.verse: “Let anyone who is thirsty come to me, and let the one who believes in me drink. As the scripture has said, ‘Out of the believer's heart shall flow rivers of living water.’”
theo: The first reading begins in a household that has gone wrong. Sarai, unable to bear children, had given her Egyptian slave-girl Hagar to Abram; Hagar conceived and looked down on her mistress; Sarai complained; and Abram washed his hands of it: “Your slave-girl is in your power; do to her as you please.” “Then Sarai dealt harshly with her, and she ran away from her.” A pregnant foreign servant, alone, runs into the desert toward Egypt. And there, of all places, “The angel of the LORD found her by a spring of water in the wilderness.” He asks her the question the Great Fast asks each of us: “Hagar, slave-girl of Sarai, where have you come from and where are you going?” He promises her a son and gives him a name, Ishmael, God hears, “for the LORD has given heed to your affliction.” Then Hagar does something no one in Scripture has done before her: she gives God a name. “So she named the LORD who spoke to her, ‘You are El-roi’; for she said, ‘Have I really seen God and remained alive after seeing him?’” El-roi, the God who sees. The first person in the Bible to name God is not a patriarch or a priest, but a runaway slave woman. Thousands of women from Kerala work as housemaids and carers far from home, some of them treated harshly behind closed doors where no one sees. God sees. And he asks us whether we see them too, in our own homes, in the women who work for us, and in the women of our families whose hurts are hidden.

The second reading finishes last Friday's story. Three days after the treaty, Israel discovers that the Gibeonites are neighbours, not travellers from afar. The congregation murmurs, but the leaders hold firm: “We have sworn to them by the LORD, the God of Israel, and now we must not touch them.” An oath made in God's name is kept, even when it was obtained by a trick and even when it costs. The psalm praises the one “who stand by their oath even to their hurt” (Psalm 15:4). Our marriage vows, our baptismal promises and our word given in business are to be kept the same way. And notice how the story ends. The Gibeonites are spared, and Joshua makes them “hewers of wood and drawers of water for the congregation and for the altar of the LORD.” The outsiders who came with mouldy bread end their story beside the altar of the God of Israel. Christian readers have seen in this wood and water carried to the altar a hint of the wood of the Cross and the water of Baptism, by which God brings strangers near to his altar.

Paul now turns from the mercy of God to the life it makes possible: “I appeal to you therefore, brothers and sisters, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship. Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your minds.” This is what the Great Fast is for. We do not fast because the body is bad, but because the body is to be offered: eyes, tongue, hands, appetite and time placed on the altar with Christ. And the sacrifice is not private. “For as in one body we have many members, and not all the members have the same function, so we, who are many, are one body in Christ, and individually we are members one of another.” Paul ends with a list that could hang on the wall of every Christian home: “Let love be genuine; hate what is evil, hold fast to what is good; love one another with mutual affection; outdo one another in showing honor. Do not lag in zeal, be ardent in spirit, serve the Lord.”

The Gospel takes us to the festival of Booths in Jerusalem. During the feast, as Jewish tradition describes it, water was carried in procession from the pool of Siloam and poured out at the altar, and great lamps were lit in the temple courts so that the whole city glowed. Into that water and that light Jesus speaks. “On the last day of the festival, the great day, while Jesus was standing there, he cried out, ‘Let anyone who is thirsty come to me, and let the one who believes in me drink.’” John explains: “Now he said this about the Spirit, which believers in him were to receive.” Then, in the treasury near the great lamps, he says: “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will never walk in darkness but will have the light of life.” Water and light: these are the two signs of our Baptism, the Mamodisa, when we were washed in water and a burning candle was placed in our hands. At the Easter Vigil the Church will bless the water and carry the new light into a dark church, and those preparing for Baptism will receive both. Hagar found a spring in the desert and met the God who sees; the Gibeonites carried water to the altar; Christ himself is the spring from which rivers of living water flow, and the light that the darkness cannot overcome. His hour “had not yet come”, but it is coming: on the Cross water will flow from his side, and on Easter morning the light will rise.
conn: Hagar's wells.

Hagar meets the angel by a spring (Genesis 16:7); later, when her child is dying of thirst, “God opened her eyes and she saw a well of water” (Genesis 21:19). At another well Jesus promises a Samaritan woman “a spring of water gushing up to eternal life” (John 4:14).
The God who sees.
Hagar calls God El-roi, the God who sees (Genesis 16:13). Jesus teaches that the Father “who sees in secret will reward you” (Matthew 6:6).
An oath kept.

Israel keeps the oath sworn to Gibeon (Joshua 9:19); the psalm blesses those “who stand by their oath even to their hurt” (Psalm 15:4). Centuries later God avenged the Gibeonites when Saul broke that oath (2 Samuel 21:1–2).
Servants at the altar.
The Gibeonites become hewers of wood and drawers of water for the altar (Joshua 9:27). The Son of Man “came not to be served but to serve” (Mark 10:45).
Rivers from the temple.
Ezekiel sees water flowing from below the threshold of the temple, south of the altar (Ezekiel 47:1). Jesus is the new temple; from his pierced side “blood and water came out” (John 19:34).
The great light.
“The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light” (Isaiah 9:2). In Christ “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not overcome it” (John 1:5).
altar: At the Holy Qurbana our bodies, our work and our fasting are placed with Christ on the altar as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God.
The Holy Qurbana is the spring of living water in the desert of the fast: the Spirit is poured out, and the Lord who is the light of the world gives himself as food.
outline: Opening
Ask: where have I come from, and where am I going?
Point 1 · El-roi
The God who sees a runaway slave woman in the desert.
Point 2 · Wood and water for the altar
An oath kept, and outsiders brought near.
Point 3 · A living sacrifice
Bodies offered, minds renewed, love genuine.
Point 4 · Living water and light
The feast of Booths, and the signs of our Baptism.
Closing image
A spring in the desert, and a candle carried into a dark church at Easter.
Take-home line
“Let anyone who is thirsty come to me.”
live: See as God sees (Genesis 16:13)
Notice one person this week who works for you or serves you unseen: a domestic worker, a driver, a cleaner. Thank them by name, pay them justly, and pray for them.
Keep your word (Joshua 9:19)
Fulfil one promise you have delayed, to God, to your spouse, to a child or to a colleague.
Offer your body (Romans 12:1)
Choose one discipline for eyes, tongue or hands this week and offer it each morning as a living sacrifice.
Renew your Baptism (John 7:37–38; 8:12)
Find out the date of your Baptism, light a candle at home that evening, and renew your baptismal promises as a family.
fathers: St John Chrysostom (in substance)

How can the body become a sacrifice? Let the eye look on nothing evil, and it has become a sacrifice; let the tongue speak nothing shameful, and it has become an offering; let the hand do nothing unlawful, and it has become a whole burnt offering. And let the hand also do good, giving alms, so that the sacrifice is complete.
St Augustine (in substance)

The Lord cries out: if anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. We come to him not by walking but by believing, not with the feet but with love. Whoever drinks from him becomes himself a spring, for love overflows from the heart to others.
magis: Catechism 2031
The moral life is spiritual worship: we present our bodies as a living sacrifice, and in the Eucharist this offering is nourished.
Catechism 694
Water is a sign of the Holy Spirit; the Spirit is the living water welling up from Christ crucified, in whom we drink.
Catechism 2715
Contemplation is a gaze of faith fixed on Jesus: “I look at him and he looks at me.”
Catechism 2150
An oath takes God as witness to what one affirms; it calls on divine truthfulness as a pledge of one's own.
Catechism 1216
Baptism is called enlightenment, because the baptised become children of light, and indeed light themselves.
saints: This week

8–13 Mar: fifth week of the Great Fast. 12 Mar: Fifth Friday of the Great Fast (abstinence; Way of the Cross). In the Latin calendar St John of God (8 Mar) and St Frances of Rome (9 Mar) are commemorated.
2027-03-07.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, spring of living water and light of the world, you are El-roi, the God who saw Hagar in the desert and who sees us now. See the hidden sufferings of the poor, the servants and the strangers, and teach us to see them with your eyes. Make us faithful to our word, bring near to your altar all who are far away, and receive our bodies as a living sacrifice. Pour out your Spirit like rivers in our hearts, and let us walk in your light until we come to the light of Easter. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.

2027-03-14.title: Sixth Sunday of the Great Fast
2027-03-14.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: The Lord gave Israel the land he promised
Do not be a stumbling block to your brother
The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep
2027-03-14.alt: Season of the Great Fast (Sauma Ramba). The last Sunday before Hosanna Sunday; this week brings the Fortieth Friday.
2027-03-14.verse: I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.
theo: “When morning dawned, the angels urged Lot, saying, ‘Get up, take your wife and your two daughters who are here, or else you will be consumed in the punishment of the city.’” The prophet Ezekiel would later name the sin of Sodom as pride, excess of food, prosperous ease, and neglect of the poor and needy (Ezekiel 16:49), and Genesis has just shown its violence against strangers. Lot knows the city is doomed, and still: “But he lingered.” It is one of the most human sentences in the Bible. We too linger at the door of conversion, knowing what we must leave and not quite leaving it. And then mercy acts: “so the men seized him and his wife and his two daughters by the hand, the LORD being merciful to him, and they brought him out and left him outside the city.” God does not wait for Lot to be brave; he takes him by the hand. Genesis adds that God did this because “God remembered Abraham” (Genesis 19:29), whose bold prayer for the city comes just before this story (Genesis 18:23–32). The command is urgent: “Flee for your life; do not look back or stop anywhere in the Plain.” Lot bargains even now for a small town nearby, and God grants it. “But Lot's wife, behind him, looked back, and she became a pillar of salt.” She was out of the city, but her heart was still in it. Jesus gave his disciples a sermon of three words on her: “Remember Lot's wife” (Luke 17:32). One week before Hosanna Sunday, the Great Fast takes us by the hand and says: do not look back, do not stop on the plain; the hills of Easter are ahead.

The second reading closes the long account of the conquest with a sentence of pure gratitude: “Thus the LORD gave to Israel all the land that he swore to their ancestors that he would give them.” And then: “Not one of all the good promises that the LORD had made to the house of Israel had failed; all came to pass.” Joshua sends the tribes who had settled east of the Jordan back to their homes, but not without a charge: “to love the LORD your God, to walk in all his ways, to keep his commandments, and to hold fast to him, and to serve him with all your heart and with all your soul.” The promised land is not the end of the covenant but a place to keep it. Paul then turns to a quarrel in the church of Rome. Some believers ate everything; others, out of conscience, would not eat meat or drink wine; each side judged the other. Paul tells the strong: “Let us therefore no longer pass judgment on one another, but resolve instead never to put a stumbling block or hindrance in the way of another.” And he gives a principle that every Lent needs: “For the kingdom of God is not food and drink but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.” Our families keep the Great Fast in different ways, from the strict fifty days of our grandparents to the lighter practice of busy young people abroad; the measure is not whose plate is emptier but whose heart is more loving. And Paul's warning reaches further: “it is good not to eat meat or drink wine or do anything that makes your brother or sister stumble.” Many families in Kerala have been wounded by drink. A father who gives up alcohol for the sake of his son, or a host who serves no liquor at a feast for the sake of one guest who struggles, is doing exactly what Paul asks: “Do not let what you eat cause the ruin of one for whom Christ died.”

In the Gospel Jesus speaks the words that the Church loves to hear at the threshold of his Passion: “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.” He contrasts himself with the hired hand who “sees the wolf coming and leaves the sheep and runs away,” because “a hired hand does not care for the sheep.” A shepherd is known by what he does when danger comes. Then he speaks of a knowledge as deep as the life of God: “I know my own and my own know me, just as the Father knows me and I know the Father. And I lay down my life for the sheep.” His gaze goes beyond the flock in front of him: “I have other sheep that do not belong to this fold. I must bring them also, and they will listen to my voice. So there will be one flock, one shepherd.” The St Thomas Christians, one Church for many centuries, have been divided into several Churches since the seventeenth century; we pray with respect and hope for the day when all will be one flock. Finally Jesus says what makes the coming week intelligible: “No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it up again.” The Passion we will celebrate is not an accident or a defeat; it is the free self-offering of the Son, who lays down his life in order to take it up again. Every bishop of our Church carries a shepherd's staff, and every priest stands at the altar to make present that one sacrifice. Let us pray for our shepherds, that they may not be hired hands, and let us listen this week for the voice of the Good Shepherd, who is already walking toward Jerusalem for us.
conn: Remember Lot's wife.
Jesus warns, “Remember Lot's wife” (Luke 17:32), and teaches that “No one who puts a hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9:62).
Abraham's prayer.

Abraham interceded for Sodom (Genesis 18:23–32), and “God remembered Abraham, and sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow” (Genesis 19:29). The prayer of the just reaches those who cannot pray for themselves.
Every promise kept.
Joshua's words, not one good promise failed (Joshua 21:45; 23:14), find their fullness in Christ, in whom “every one of God's promises is a ‘Yes’” (2 Corinthians 1:20).
With all your heart.
Joshua's charge to love the LORD and serve him with all your heart and soul (Joshua 22:5) repeats the great commandment of Deuteronomy 6:5, which Jesus called the first of all (Mark 12:29–30).
The stumbling block.
Paul makes the same choice in Corinth: “if food is a cause of their falling, I will never eat meat” (1 Corinthians 8:13); Jesus warns those who cause a little one to stumble (Matthew 18:6).
The shepherd of Israel.

The LORD is my shepherd (Psalm 23:1); God promises to seek his scattered sheep himself (Ezekiel 34:11–16); Christ is “the shepherd and guardian of your souls” (1 Peter 2:25) and “the great shepherd of the sheep” (Hebrews 13:20).
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the Good Shepherd lays down his life for the sheep: the one sacrifice of the Cross is made present on the altar, and he who laid down his life and took it up again feeds his flock with his own Body and Blood.

Around the altar the many sheep become one flock: those who keep the fast strictly and those who keep it lightly, the strong and the weak, receive the same Bread, and none may be a stumbling block to another.
outline: Opening
Ask: where am I lingering at the door, or looking back?
Point 1 · But he lingered
Mercy that takes us by the hand.
Point 2 · Not one promise failed
Holding fast in the land of promise.
Point 3 · Not food and drink
No stumbling block for a brother or sister.
Point 4 · The good shepherd
He lays down his life of his own accord.
Closing image
A woman turned to salt on the road out of the burning plain, and a shepherd walking ahead of his flock toward Jerusalem.
Take-home line
“The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.”
live: Do not look back (Genesis 19:17)
Name the one thing you keep looking back at, a habit, a resentment, a relationship, and make a definite break with it before Hosanna Sunday.
Thank God for kept promises (Joshua 21:45)
Write down three promises God has kept in your family's life, and read them aloud at the family prayer.
Remove a stumbling block (Romans 14:21)
Give up for the rest of the fast one thing, a drink, a habit of speech, a way of using the phone, that may lead someone close to you into sin.
Pray for shepherds (John 10:11)
Pray each day this week for your bishop and parish priest, and for vocations to the priesthood from your parish.
fathers: St Gregory the Great (in substance)

The hireling does not always flee by running away; he flees when he sees the wolf and keeps silent. He flees in his heart when he will not stand up for the sheep, because he loves his own comfort more than the flock.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)

Christ did not refuse to die for your brother, and will you not give up a dish of food for him? He gave his life; you are asked only to deny yourself a little meat or wine so that the one for whom he died may not fall.
magis: Catechism 609

By embracing in his human heart the Father's love for men, Jesus loved them to the end; his suffering and death were the free offering of his life: no one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord.
Catechism 754
The Church is a sheepfold whose one gate is Christ, and a flock of which God himself foretold that he would be the shepherd.
Catechism 2284
Scandal is an attitude or behaviour which leads another to do evil; it is a grave offence when by deed or omission another is deliberately led into sin.
Catechism 1817
Hope is the virtue by which we desire the kingdom of heaven and eternal life, placing our trust in Christ's promises and relying on the help of the Holy Spirit.
Catechism 1438
The seasons and days of penance, especially Lent and each Friday in memory of the Lord's death, are intense moments of the Church's penitential practice.
saints: This week

15–20 Mar: sixth week of the Great Fast. 19 Mar: Sixth Friday of the Great Fast, the Fortieth Friday (Nalpatham Velli), with St Joseph, Spouse of the Blessed Virgin Mary. 20 Mar: the Saturday before Hosanna, recalling Lazarus and the anointing at Bethany; kozhukatta are made in many homes. 21 Mar: Hosanna Sunday.
2027-03-14.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, Good Shepherd, you lay down your life for the sheep of your own accord, and you take it up again. When we linger at the door of conversion, take us by the hand as the angels took Lot, and do not let us look back. Keep us faithful to your promises, every one of which is Yes in you. Make us careful never to place a stumbling block before those for whom you died, and gather all your scattered sheep into one flock under your one staff. As you walk toward Jerusalem, let us hear your voice and follow you. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.

2027-03-21.title: Hosanna Sunday · Seventh Sunday of the Great Fast
2027-03-21.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: The scepter shall not depart from Judah
Your king comes to you, humble
Grafted into the cultivated olive tree
Hosanna to the Son of David
2027-03-21.alt: Hosanna Sunday (Oshana Njayar): the blessing of the palms, the procession and the Holy Qurbana. The Week of the Passion (Hasha Week) begins. Longer forms in the calendar: Genesis 49:1–12, 22–26; Matthew 20:29–21:22.
2027-03-21.verse: Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest heaven!
theo: Today the Church walks with Jesus into Jerusalem, and the Great Fast gives way to the Week of the Passion, which our tradition calls Hasha Week. Hosanna Sunday is one of the days Kerala Christians love most, and its rite is simple enough for every family to follow. First, the people gather before the Holy Qurbana, often outside the church or at a nearby cross, each holding a tender coconut leaf, the kuruthola. Second, the celebrant prays over the palms and blesses them, sprinkling them with holy water. Third, the Gospel of the Lord's entry into Jerusalem is proclaimed, so that we hear what we are about to do. Fourth, the procession moves toward the church and around it, with the cross going before, while everyone waves the palms and sings the Hosanna hymns, as the crowds did on the road from Bethphage. Fifth, the procession enters the church, and the Holy Qurbana continues with the readings of the day: the King we have welcomed with palms now comes to us on the altar. Afterwards the families take the blessed palms home and keep them in the prayer corner. On Pesaha a small cross folded from the blessed palm is pressed into the Pesaha appam; and many parishes keep the old palms to burn them for the ashes at the beginning of next year's Great Fast. So the palm of welcome, the bread of the Supper and the ashes of repentance are woven into one year of faith. Customs vary from eparchy to eparchy and parish to parish; follow the order your parish uses.

The first reading is the blessing of the dying Jacob over his sons. To Judah he says: “Judah, your brothers shall praise you; your hand shall be on the neck of your enemies; your father's sons shall bow down before you.” And then a promise that Israel treasured for centuries: “The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor the ruler's staff from between his feet, until tribute comes to him; and the obedience of the peoples is his.” Strangely, the next line speaks of a donkey: “Binding his foal to the vine and his donkey's colt to the choice vine, he washes his garments in wine and his robe in the blood of grapes.” The Fathers saw here the King from Judah who would come riding on a donkey's colt, and whose garments would be washed in the wine of his own blood. The reading also gives the blessing of Joseph, the son who suffered at the hands of his brothers and saved them: “Joseph is a fruitful bough, a fruitful bough by a spring; his branches run over the wall. The archers fiercely attacked him; they shot at him and pressed him hard. Yet his bow remained taut, and his arms were made agile by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob.” In the King from Judah and the rejected brother who saves his family, the Church has always seen one face: Jesus, the Son of David, who goes up to Jerusalem to be rejected and to save.

Zechariah's prophecy is the key to everything that happens on the road from Bethany: “Rejoice greatly, O daughter Zion! Shout aloud, O daughter Jerusalem! Lo, your king comes to you; triumphant and victorious is he, humble and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey.” Kings rode into cities on war horses. This King comes on a farmer's animal, and the prophet explains why: “He will cut off the chariot from Ephraim and the war-horse from Jerusalem; and the battle bow shall be cut off, and he shall command peace to the nations.” He wins his kingdom not by killing but by dying, and he seals it “because of the blood of my covenant with you”. And he calls out to all who are trapped: “Return to your stronghold, O prisoners of hope.” In Kerala, where elephants and caparisons and loud processions mark our feasts, the Lord's chosen mount is a quiet rebuke and a great comfort. He does not come to frighten us; he comes humble, to set prisoners free.

Paul, writing to Gentile Christians in Rome, uses an image every Kerala farmer understands: grafting. The Church of Israel is a cultivated olive tree with a holy root. Some branches were broken off; the Gentiles, “a wild olive shoot”, have been grafted in “to share the rich root of the olive tree”. Paul's warning is sharp: “do not boast over the branches. If you do boast, remember that it is not you that support the root, but the root that supports you.” “So do not become proud, but stand in awe.” And he insists that God has not finished with his people: “God has the power to graft them in again.” This reading belongs on Hosanna Sunday. As we enter the Week of the Passion, the Church forbids us to blame the Jewish people as a whole for the death of Jesus; the Second Vatican Council teaches that the Jews remain most dear to God, whose gifts and call are irrevocable, and that his Passion cannot be charged against all the Jews of that time or of today. Christ died for the sins of all of us, and we are the branches who live from the root.

Then the Gospel. Jesus sends two disciples to bring a donkey and her colt, and Matthew tells us why: “This took place to fulfill what had been spoken through the prophet.” The crowds spread their cloaks on the road, cut branches from the trees, and shout: “Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest heaven!” Hosanna is a Hebrew cry meaning “Save us, we pray”, taken from Psalm 118, the pilgrims' psalm. “When he entered Jerusalem, the whole city was in turmoil, asking, ‘Who is this?’” That question will echo through the whole week. Matthew goes straight on to the temple: Jesus drives out the sellers and buyers and overturns the tables, saying, “It is written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer’; but you are making it a den of robbers.” Then “the blind and the lame came to him in the temple, and he cured them”, and the children go on crying “Hosanna to the Son of David”. When the authorities object, Jesus quotes the psalm: “Out of the mouths of infants and nursing babies you have prepared praise for yourself.” The King's first act in his city is to cleanse the house of prayer and to heal; and the purest praise comes from children. Today, as our children wave their palms, let us ask whether our own hearts, our homes and our parishes are houses of prayer, and whether the cry Hosanna on our lips today will still be there on Friday.
conn: The foal bound to the vine.
Jacob's blessing speaks of Judah binding his donkey's colt to the vine (Genesis 49:11); Jesus sends for a donkey tied with her colt and rides into Jerusalem (Matthew 21:2–7).
The humble king.
Zechariah's king comes humble, riding on a donkey (Zechariah 9:9), quoted at the entry (Matthew 21:5; John 12:14–15). Solomon too rode David's mule to be anointed king (1 Kings 1:33–39).
Hosanna.

The crowd's cry comes from the pilgrims' psalm: “Save us, we beseech you, O Lord … Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord” (Psalm 118:25–26). The Church sings it in the Holy Qurbana before the Lord comes on the altar.
Cloaks and branches.

Cloaks were spread for Jehu when he was proclaimed king (2 Kings 9:13); palms and branches were carried when the temple was purified in the days of the Maccabees (2 Maccabees 10:7). John tells that the crowd took branches of palm trees (John 12:13).
A house of prayer.

Jesus joins Isaiah, “my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples” (Isaiah 56:7), and Jeremiah's warning against making it “a den of robbers” (Jeremiah 7:11). His own body is the new temple (John 2:19–21).
The root that supports you.

Paul's olive tree (Romans 11:17–24) is echoed by the Second Vatican Council: the Church draws sustenance from the root of that good olive tree onto which the Gentiles have been grafted (Nostra Aetate 4).
altar: The King who entered Jerusalem humble and riding on a donkey enters our church in the procession, and then comes truly on the altar in the Holy Qurbana; the Hosanna we sing before the anaphora greets the same Lord.
In the Holy Qurbana we receive the blood of the covenant of which Zechariah spoke, the blood that sets the prisoners of hope free.
outline: Opening
Ask: will my Hosanna today still be on my lips on Friday?
Point 1 · The scepter of Judah
The promised King from the line of David.
Point 2 · Humble and riding on a donkey
A King of peace, not of war horses.
Point 3 · A house of prayer
The King cleanses the temple and heals.
Point 4 · The root supports you
Grafted in by grace; no room for pride.
Closing image
Children waving coconut leaves at the church door, and a cross of folded palm pressed into the Pesaha appam.
Take-home line
“Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord!”
live: Keep the blessed palm (Matthew 21:8)
Place the blessed palm in your prayer corner, and fold a small cross from it for the Pesaha appam on Thursday.
Make the house a house of prayer (Matthew 21:13)
Gather the family for prayer every evening this week, and keep the house quieter, with less noise and screen time.
Follow every day of the week
Plan now to attend the services of Pesaha, Passion Friday, Great Saturday and the Easter vigil and Qurbana, and bring the children.
Learn humility (Romans 11:20)
Refuse every word of contempt this week, against other Christians, against the Jewish people, against anyone.
fathers: St Andrew of Crete (in substance)

Let us go together to meet Christ on the Mount of Olives. Let us spread before his feet not garments or lifeless branches, but ourselves, clothed in his grace; and let us wave, not palm branches, but the palms of victory, crying with the children: Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel.
St Augustine (in substance)

It was no promotion for the King of the ages to become the King of Israel; it was condescension. He did not come to exact tribute or to command armies, but to rule souls, to lead to heaven those who believe, hope and love.
magis: Catechism 559
Jesus entered Jerusalem as the Messiah, Son of David, riding on a donkey; he is acclaimed by children and the poor, and the Church takes up their Hosanna in the Sanctus of the liturgy.
Catechism 560
Jesus' entry into Jerusalem manifested the coming of the kingdom that the King-Messiah was going to accomplish by the Passover of his death and Resurrection; with it the Church begins Holy Week.
Catechism 584
Jesus went up to the temple as the privileged place of encounter with God; he was angered that its outer court had become a place of commerce.
Catechism 597–598
The historical complexity of Jesus' trial means that the Jews as a whole cannot be held responsible for his death; all sinners were the authors of his Passion.
Second Vatican Council, Nostra Aetate 4

The Church draws sustenance from the root of that good olive tree onto which the Gentiles have been grafted; the Jews remain most dear to God, and what happened in his Passion cannot be charged against all the Jews then living, nor against the Jews of today.
saints: This week

The Week of the Passion (Hasha Week). 22–24 Mar: Monday to Wednesday of the Week of the Passion. 25 Mar: Pesaha, the Holy Qurbana of the Lord's Supper with the washing of feet (one Qurbana in each church); at home, the Pesaha appam and paal. The Annunciation (25 Mar) falls on Pesaha this year and is transferred as the Syro-Malabar Ordo directs (verify locally). 26 Mar: Passion Friday (Dukha Velli): the Way of the Cross, the veneration of the Cross, the bitter drink (kaippuneer). 27 Mar: Great Saturday. 28 Mar: Easter, the Resurrection (Uyirppu).
2027-03-21.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of David and King of peace, you came to Jerusalem humble and riding on a donkey, and the children cried Hosanna. Today we take up their cry: save us, we pray. Cleanse the temple of our hearts and make our homes houses of prayer. Keep us humble, grafted by grace into the olive tree of your people, and let our Hosanna not fall silent when the week grows dark, but follow you to the Cross and to the joy of your Resurrection. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.

2027-03-25.title: Pesaha Thursday · Holy Qurbana of the Lord's Supper
2027-03-25.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: A pure offering among the nations
The institution of the Lord's Supper
The washing of the feet and the institution of the Holy Qurbana
2027-03-25.alt: Hasha Week. Pesaha: only one Holy Qurbana is celebrated in each church, with the Order of the third Qudasha (named in the calendar after Mar Nestorius); outside the Qurbana, Holy Communion is given today only to the sick. The Annunciation (25 March) falls on Pesaha this year and is transferred as the Syro-Malabar Ordo directs (verify locally); in the Latin calendar it moves to Monday 5 April.
2027-03-25.verse: Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end.
theo: Pesaha is the Aramaic and Syriac form of the Hebrew Pesach, the Passover. For the St Thomas Christians the word names this whole holy Thursday: the night the Lord ate the Passover with his disciples, gave us the Holy Qurbana and the priesthood, and washed their feet. Tonight every parish gathers around one altar, and every home around one table. The first reading takes us back to the night in Egypt. “This month shall mark for you the beginning of months”: the Passover begins a new year and a new life. Each household is to take “a lamb for each family”, and if a household is too small, “it shall join its closest neighbor”. The lamb must be “without blemish, a year-old male”. At twilight it is slaughtered, and its blood is put “on the two doorposts and the lintel of the houses in which they eat it.” They eat it “roasted over the fire with unleavened bread and bitter herbs”, dressed for a journey: “your loins girded, your sandals on your feet, and your staff in your hand; and you shall eat it hurriedly. It is the passover of the LORD.” God promises, “when I see the blood, I will pass over you”, and he commands, “This day shall be a day of remembrance for you.” For seven days no leaven may be found in their houses. Every detail points to tonight. Jesus is the Lamb without blemish, whom John the Baptist had called “the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29), and Paul writes, “For our paschal lamb, Christ, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). The unleavened bread of Israel's haste becomes the unleavened appam of our Pesaha table, and the memorial of the Exodus becomes the memorial of a greater exodus: from sin and death to the Father.

The second reading, from the last of the prophets, is a sharp rebuke. The priests of Malachi's time offered God what they would not have dared to offer a governor, bringing as their offering “what has been taken by violence or is lame or sick”, and they treated the Lord's table with contempt. God cries out: “Oh, that someone among you would shut the temple doors, so that you would not kindle fire on my altar in vain!” Then comes a promise that looks far beyond Jerusalem: “For from the rising of the sun to its setting my name is great among the nations, and in every place incense is offered to my name, and a pure offering”. From the first century the Church heard in these words a prophecy of the Holy Qurbana. The Didache, one of the oldest Christian writings, recalls Malachi when it tells believers to confess their sins and be reconciled before they break bread on the Lord's Day, so that their sacrifice may be pure; St Justin and St Irenaeus taught that the pure offering made in every place is the Eucharist of the Church among the nations. When the Pesaha Qurbana is celebrated tonight in Kerala, in the Gulf, in Europe, in America and in Australia, from the rising of the sun to its setting, Malachi's word is fulfilled. His warning also stands: the Lord deserves our best and not what is left over, and we come to his altar tonight with hearts made clean.

Paul gives us the oldest written account of the Supper, set down about twenty-five years after that night: “For I received from the Lord what I also handed on to you, that the Lord Jesus on the night when he was betrayed took a loaf of bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it and said, ‘This is my body that is for you. Do this in remembrance of me.’ In the same way he took the cup also, after supper, saying, ‘This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me.’” Matthew, read together with John tonight, gives the words of the covenant: “Take, eat; this is my body.” “Drink from it, all of you; for this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins.” Jesus does not say: this is a sign of my body. He says: this is my body. The Church has always believed that by the word of Christ and the power of the Holy Spirit the bread and wine become truly, really and substantially his Body and Blood (Catechism 1374–1376), and that the Qurbana is the memorial of his sacrifice, in which the one sacrifice of the Cross is made present (Catechism 1362–1367). That is why Paul is so serious: “For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes.” And: “Examine yourselves, and only then eat of the bread and drink of the cup. For all who eat and drink without discerning the body, eat and drink judgment against themselves.” Tonight we also thank God for the priesthood. When Jesus said, Do this in remembrance of me, he made his apostles priests of the new covenant (Catechism 611, 1337). Then, Matthew tells us, “When they had sung the hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.” The Supper leads straight to Gethsemane and the Cross.

John, who does not tell of the bread and the cup, tells instead what Jesus did at the same table. “Now before the festival of the Passover, Jesus knew that his hour had come to depart from this world and go to the Father. Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end.” Knowing “that the Father had given all things into his hands”, the Lord of all “got up from the table, took off his outer robe, and tied a towel around himself. Then he poured water into a basin and began to wash the disciples' feet”. In that world it was the work of a slave. Peter protests: “You will never wash my feet.” Jesus answers: “Unless I wash you, you have no share with me.” Peter, all or nothing as always, cries: “Lord, not my feet only but also my hands and my head!” Jesus washes even the feet of Judas, knowing who was to betray him. Then he sits down again and explains: “So if I, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another's feet. For I have set you an example, that you also should do as I have done to you.” By reading John and Matthew together tonight, the Syro-Malabar Church teaches us that the altar and the basin belong together. The One who gives us his Body and Blood is the One who kneels at our feet. A Qurbana that does not lead us to serve has not yet reached our hands and feet.

How the parish keeps Pesaha, step by step (customs vary; follow your own parish). First, one Qurbana: in each church only one Holy Qurbana is celebrated today, usually in the afternoon or evening, so that the whole parish gathers around one altar as the apostles gathered around one table. The calendar directs the Order of the third Qudasha, used only on a few great days of the year. Outside this Qurbana, Holy Communion is taken today only to the sick. Second, the Word: the four readings are proclaimed, the Passover lamb, Malachi's pure offering, Paul's account of the Supper, and the Gospel of the washing of the feet and the institution. Third, the washing of the feet: usually after the Gospel and the homily, the celebrant lays aside his outer vestment, ties a towel around himself and kneels before twelve persons chosen from the parish, who represent the apostles. He pours water over the feet of each, dries them and kisses them, while the choir sings the hymns of the Lord's humility. Watch the priest kneel, and remember who knelt first. Fourth, the Qurbana continues: the gifts are brought to the altar, the anaphora is prayed, and the Lord's own words over the bread and the cup are spoken on the very night on which he first spoke them. Fifth, Communion: prepare with a good confession, and receive with reverence, discerning the body. Sixth, the watch: in many parishes the Blessed Sacrament is honoured with adoration far into the night, in answer to the Lord's question in Gethsemane: “So, could you not stay awake with me one hour?” (Matthew 26:40). Come for at least one hour.

How the family keeps Pesaha at home, step by step. The Syro-Malabar home has its own Pesaha, cherished for generations, which many see as a living echo of Israel's Passover meal. First, the appam: during the day the mother of the family, often with the children, prepares the Pesaha appam, an unleavened bread of rice flour (in many places with roasted urad dal and grated coconut), steamed and never leavened, because the Lord ate the Passover with unleavened bread. The little cross made from Hosanna Sunday's palm is pressed on top. In many places it is called the INRI appam, from the letters placed above the Cross. Second, the paal: Pesaha paal is coconut milk boiled with jaggery and a little cardamom or dry ginger, sweet and dark, to be eaten with the appam. Third, the gathering: in the evening, after the parish Qurbana, the whole family gathers around the table or on a mat, with a lamp lit. Fourth, prayer and the Word: the head of the family leads the prayers, the account of the Supper or of the washing of the feet is read (John 13 or 1 Corinthians 11), and the family sings a hymn and prays a psalm. Fifth, the breaking: the father, or the eldest member, breaks the appam, dips each piece in the paal and gives it to each member of the household in order of age. Sixth, the meaning: this is not a Qurbana and not a second Eucharist, but a family memorial and a holy custom, which gathers the house around the Lord's Supper that the parish has just celebrated. In many places a house in mourning does not make its own appam that year, and neighbours or relatives share theirs with it. In the Gulf and in distant lands, families who cannot find all the old ingredients keep the custom anyway, and children who have never seen Kerala learn this night by heart.
conn: Pesach, Pesaha.
The Hebrew Pesach means passing over (Exodus 12:13); the Syriac Pesaha gives its name to this Thursday and to the appam and paal of the home.
The Lamb without blemish.
No bone of the Passover lamb was to be broken (Exodus 12:46); John sees this fulfilled on the Cross: “None of his bones shall be broken” (John 19:36).
Unleavened bread.
Paul tells Christians to celebrate the festival not with the old yeast of malice and evil, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (1 Corinthians 5:8).
The pure offering.
Malachi 1:11 is quoted in the Didache (chapter 14) and by St Justin and St Irenaeus as a prophecy of the Eucharist offered among the nations.
The blood of the covenant.
Moses sealed the covenant with blood at Sinai (Exodus 24:8); Jeremiah promised a new covenant (Jeremiah 31:31); Jesus says, This is my blood of the covenant (Matthew 26:28).
The hymn.
At the Passover meal the Hallel psalms (Psalms 113–118) were sung; among them Psalm 116, I will lift up the cup of salvation, which Jesus would have sung with his disciples on this night.
One who serves.
At the Supper Jesus says, I am among you as one who serves (Luke 22:27); he came not to be served but to serve (Mark 10:45).
The Annunciation transferred.
The Word was made flesh in Mary's womb so that he could give his flesh for the life of the world (John 6:51); the feast is transferred this year, but the two mysteries belong together.
altar: Tonight at the Holy Qurbana the Lord's words are spoken on the night on which he first spoke them: This is my body; this is my blood. What he did in the upper room, he does on our altar.
The Lamb whose blood marked the doorposts in Egypt is the Lamb on our altar; the blood of the new covenant is not put on our doors but given to us to drink.
Malachi's pure offering is made tonight from the rising of the sun to its setting, wherever the Syro-Malabar Church celebrates the Pesaha Qurbana.
outline: Opening
Ask: what does it mean that the Lord loved his own to the end, and that I am one of his own?
Point 1 · The blood on the doorposts
The Passover lamb and our paschal Lamb.
Point 2 · A pure offering in every place
Malachi's promise and the Qurbana of the nations.
Point 3 · This is my body
The Real Presence, the sacrifice, the priesthood.
Point 4 · Wash one another's feet
The altar and the basin belong together.
Closing image
A priest kneeling with a towel and a basin, and a father breaking the Pesaha appam for his children.
Take-home line
“Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end.”
live: Come to the one Qurbana
Let the whole family come together to the Pesaha Qurbana of your parish, and arrive early.
Discern the body (1 Corinthians 11:28)
If you have not yet made your confession, make it before the Qurbana, and receive Communion with reverence.
Keep the home Pesaha
Prepare the appam and paal together, read John 13 at the table, and let the eldest break the bread for all.
Wash one another's feet (John 13:14)
Do one humble service at home tonight that is usually left to someone else, without being asked.
Watch one hour (Matthew 26:40)
Spend an hour in adoration before the Blessed Sacrament tonight, or a quiet hour of prayer at home.
fathers: St John Chrysostom (in substance)

It is not a man who makes the gifts become the Body and Blood of Christ, but Christ himself, who was crucified for us. The priest stands there fulfilling the figure and speaking the words; the power and the grace are God's. This is my body, he says, and that word transforms the gifts.
St Cyril of Jerusalem (in substance)
Do not regard the bread and wine as plain bread and wine, for they are the Body and Blood of Christ, as the Lord has declared. Even if the senses suggest otherwise, let faith make you firm.
St Ephrem the Syrian (in substance)
In your bread is hidden the Spirit who is not consumed; in your wine dwells the fire that is not drunk. The Lord who washed the feet of his disciples gave them his own Body with the same hands.
St Augustine (in substance)
The Lord washed the feet of his disciples to teach us that we must do for one another what he did for us; and he gave us his Body so that we, many as we are, may become one body.
magis: Catechism 1337

The Lord, having loved those who were his own, loved them to the end. Knowing that the hour had come, he washed their feet and gave the commandment of love, and he instituted the Eucharist as the memorial of his death and Resurrection.
Catechism 1340

By celebrating the Last Supper with his apostles in the course of the Passover meal, Jesus gave the Jewish Passover its definitive meaning: his passing over to the Father by his death and Resurrection.
Catechism 1366–1367
The Eucharist is a sacrifice because it makes present the sacrifice of the Cross; the sacrifice of Christ and the sacrifice of the Eucharist are one single sacrifice.
Catechism 1374
In the Eucharist the Body and Blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, together with his soul and divinity, and therefore the whole Christ, is truly, really and substantially contained.
Catechism 611
By the words Do this in remembrance of me, Jesus instituted his apostles as priests of the New Covenant.
Lumen Gentium 11
Taking part in the Eucharistic sacrifice, the source and summit of the whole Christian life, the faithful offer the divine Victim to God, and themselves along with it.
saints: The Annunciation
This year 25 March falls on Pesaha. The feast of the Annunciation is transferred as the Syro-Malabar Ordo directs (verify locally); in the Latin calendar it is kept on Monday 5 April 2027.
The coming days

26 Mar: Passion Friday (Dukha Velli), with fasting and abstinence, the bitter drink (kaippuneer), the Way of the Cross and the veneration of the Cross. 27 Mar: Great Saturday. 28 Mar: Easter, the Uyirppu of the Lord.
2027-03-25.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, Lamb of God without blemish, on the night you were betrayed you took bread and the cup and gave us your Body and Blood, and you knelt to wash the feet of your disciples. Having loved your own, you loved them to the end. Make us worthy to receive you tonight with clean hearts, discerning your Body. Bless the priests you have chosen to do this in your memory. Teach us to wash one another's feet, to watch with you in Gethsemane, and to follow you through the Cross to the joy of your Resurrection. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.

2027-03-26.title: Passion Friday (Good Friday)
2027-03-26.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: The Passion of Christ (Part II): the pierced side and the burial
2027-03-26.alt: Passion Friday (Dukha Velli). A day of fasting and abstinence. There is no celebration of the Holy Qurbana today; the Church keeps the service of the Passion, the veneration of the Cross, the procession and the burial of the Cross. The order and the hours follow your diocese and parish.
2027-03-26.verse: When Jesus had received the wine, he said, “It is finished.” Then he bowed his head and gave up his spirit.
theo: The Church begins this day of sorrow with a father and a son climbing a mountain. God says to Abraham, “Take your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love, and go to the land of Moriah, and offer him there as a burnt offering on one of the mountains that I shall show you.” Every word tightens the knot: your son, your only son, whom you love. Abraham lays the wood on Isaac's shoulders and carries the fire and the knife himself, “So the two of them walked on together.” Then the boy asks the question that echoes through the whole Bible: “The fire and the wood are here, but where is the lamb for a burnt offering?” Abraham answers, “God himself will provide the lamb for a burnt offering, my son.” On Moriah the hand of Abraham is stopped and a ram caught in a thicket dies in Isaac's place. On Calvary no hand is stopped. The Father does not spare his own Son, and the Son carries the wood of his own sacrifice up the hill. The question of Isaac is answered at last by John the Baptist: “Here is the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world!” What Abraham was asked to give and was spared, God gives and does not spare. That is why the Church reads Genesis 22 today: to show that the Cross is not a human tragedy that God turned to good, but the gift of the Father who so loved the world that he gave his only Son.

Isaiah's fourth song of the Servant is read on this day by Christians everywhere, because it reads like an eyewitness account written centuries before. “He was despised and rejected by others; a man of suffering and acquainted with infirmity.” The prophet's community confesses its mistake: they thought he was punished by God for his own sins. Then the truth breaks in: “But he was wounded for our transgressions, crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the punishment that made us whole, and by his bruises we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray; we have all turned to our own way, and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all.” And the Servant goes silent to his death: “like a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and like a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he did not open his mouth.” Paul draws out what this means for us. Christ did not die for the good and the deserving: “For while we were still weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly.” “But God proves his love for us in that while we still were sinners Christ died for us.” The Cross is the proof. Whoever doubts that God loves him should look at the crucifix and read what is written there: you were worth this to me. And Paul goes further: through one man's disobedience sin and death entered; through the one man Jesus Christ the free gift of grace overflows to the many.

The Passion is read today in two parts, woven from the Gospels of Luke, Matthew and John. Jesus is mocked, blindfolded and struck; he is led to the council, to Pilate, to Herod, and back to Pilate. Three times Pilate finds no case against him. Pilate's wife sends a message: “Have nothing to do with that innocent man, for today I have suffered a great deal because of a dream about him.” Pilate washes his hands, and the crowd cries, “His blood be on us and on our children!” The Church reads these words with great care. The Second Vatican Council teaches that what happened in the Passion “cannot be charged against all the Jews, without distinction, then alive, nor against the Jews of today” (Nostra Aetate 4), and the Catechism reminds us that sinners, all of us, were the authors of Christ's sufferings (CCC 597–598). Indeed the blood of Christ is on us: not as a curse but as the blood that cleanses, sprinkled on all who are saved. Then come the words from the Cross. To his executioners: “Father, forgive them; for they do not know what they are doing.” To the thief who asks to be remembered: “Truly I tell you, today you will be with me in Paradise.” To his Mother and the beloved disciple: “Woman, here is your son… Here is your mother.” Then, “I am thirsty”, and they lift a sponge of sour wine to his lips. “It is finished.” Darkness covers the land, the curtain of the temple is torn, the earth shakes, and a Roman officer says, “Truly this man was God's Son!” In the second part a soldier pierces his side, “and at once blood and water came out”, and Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus lay him in a new tomb in a garden. The Fathers saw in that blood and water the Holy Qurbana and Baptism, and the Church herself born from the side of the new Adam asleep on the Cross.

How a family can follow the rites of Passion Friday, step by step (the order and names differ a little between dioceses, so follow your parish). First, the fast: on this day the faithful keep fast and abstinence, and many keep silence, switch off the television and take only kanji. Second, the service of the Passion in church, usually in the morning or afternoon: the prayers of the day, the readings from Genesis, Isaiah and Romans, and the long reading of the Passion (Part I), followed by the Passion sermon. There is no Holy Qurbana on this day: the altar stands bare, for the one Sacrifice is contemplated on the Cross itself. Third, the veneration of the Cross (Sliva Vandanam): the crucifix is shown to the people, and one by one they come forward, kneel and kiss the wounds of the Lord. Fourth, the procession with the Cross through the streets or around the church, praying the Way of the Cross; many walk to hills of pilgrimage such as Malayattoor with wooden crosses on their shoulders. Fifth, the second part of the Passion (John 19:31–42) and the burial: the body of the Lord, the crucifix or an image, is laid in a tomb prepared with flowers, and the people pass by in prayer. Sixth, the bitter drink (kaippuneer): at the end each one takes a sip of a bitter drink, recalling the sour wine offered to the thirsty Lord on the Cross, and promising to share his bitterness rather than run from it. At home, many families read or sing the Puthen Pana of Arnos Pathiri, especially the lament of the Mother, and keep the evening in quiet. Nothing in these rites is theatre. Each step is a way of standing with Mary and John at the foot of the Cross, where the world was redeemed.
conn: Isaac and the Lamb.
Isaac carries the wood up Moriah (Genesis 22:6); Jesus goes out “carrying the cross by himself” (John 19:17). The ram dies in Isaac's place; the Lamb of God dies in ours (John 1:29).
The Passover Lamb.
Not one bone of the Passover lamb was to be broken (Exodus 12:46); John sees this fulfilled when the soldiers do not break the legs of Jesus (John 19:36).
Thirst and vinegar.
“For my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Psalm 69:21); on the Cross Jesus says “I am thirsty” and receives the sour wine (John 19:28–30). The kaippuneer of Passion Friday keeps this memory.
The cry of the Psalm.
“My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Psalm 22:1; Matthew 27:46) is the first line of a psalm that ends in praise and the conversion of the nations (Psalm 22:27).
The torn curtain.
The curtain that hid the Holy of Holies is torn (Matthew 27:51); through his flesh Christ has opened for us a new and living way into the sanctuary (Hebrews 10:19–20).
The new Adam's side.
As Eve was formed from the side of the sleeping Adam (Genesis 2:21–22), the Church is born from the opened side of Christ: blood and water, the Eucharist and Baptism (John 19:34).
altar: Today there is no Holy Qurbana, and the bare altar teaches as loudly as any sermon. The sacrifice we offer every Sunday is not another sacrifice but this one: the one offering of Calvary made present on the altar under the signs of bread and wine.

When we kiss the Cross today, we kiss the same Lord we receive in Holy Communion. The Body that hung on the tree is the Body that is given to us; the Blood that flowed from his side is the Blood in the chalice.
outline: Opening
Silence before the Cross. Ask: what did my salvation cost?
Point 1 · God will provide the lamb
Moriah and Calvary: the Father who does not spare his Son.
Point 2 · By his bruises we are healed
The Servant who bore our sins in silence.
Point 3 · The words from the Cross
Forgiveness, Paradise, a Mother, thirst, completion.
Point 4 · Blood and water
The Church born from his side; kneeling with Mary.
Closing image
A family in a dark church, waiting in line to kiss the feet of the crucified Lord, and a child lifted up to kiss them too.
Take-home line
“It is finished.”
live: Keep the fast with love
Fast and abstain today, and offer the hunger for someone who suffers.
Forgive (Luke 23:34)
Name one person who has hurt you and pray today: Father, forgive them.
Kiss the Cross
Take part in the service of the Passion and the veneration of the Cross with your whole family.
Keep the evening quiet
Read the Passion (John 19) or the Puthen Pana at home, and leave the television and phone aside.
fathers: St Ephrem the Syrian (in substance)

Death trampled our Lord underfoot, but he in turn treated death as a highroad for his own feet. He submitted to death of his own will, so that he might overthrow death against death's will. He went out to Golgotha carrying his Cross, and from the Cross he called the dead out of Sheol.
St Melito of Sardis (in substance)

He who hung the earth in its place is hanged; he who fixed the heavens is fixed to a tree; the Master is insulted, God is murdered. He is the Lamb that was slain and taken from the flock, and he has rescued us from slavery to freedom, from darkness to light, from death to life.
magis: Catechism 599–600
Jesus' violent death was not the result of chance; it belongs to the mystery of God's plan, which also uses human sin for our salvation.
Catechism 597–598
The Passion cannot be charged against all Jews of that time or of today; all sinners were the authors of Christ's sufferings.
Catechism 613–614
The death of Christ is both the Paschal sacrifice and the sacrifice of the New Covenant; it is unique and completes all other sacrifices.
Catechism 616
It is love to the end that gives Christ's sacrifice its value of redemption and reparation.
Catechism 964
Mary's union with her Son in the work of salvation is shown at the foot of the Cross.
Catechism 766
The Church was born from the pierced side of Christ asleep on the Cross.
saints: Holy Week
Saturday 27 March: Great Saturday. Sunday 28 March: the Resurrection of our Lord (Uyirppu). Monday 29 to Saturday 3 April: the first week of Resurrection, the week of the newly baptised.
2027-03-26.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, Lamb of God, you carried the wood of your sacrifice up the hill, and you were wounded for our transgressions. We adore you and we bless you, for by your holy Cross you have redeemed the world. Forgive us as you forgave those who crucified you; remember us in your kingdom as you remembered the thief; give us your Mother as you gave her to the beloved disciple. Let the blood and water from your side wash us and feed us, and let us not run from your Cross but stand beside it with Mary, until we see your glory. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.

2027-03-27.title: Great Saturday
2027-03-27.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Jonah in the belly of the fish three days and three nights
United with Christ in his death and resurrection
The good news of the Resurrection
2027-03-27.alt: Great Saturday. The Lord rests in the tomb. In many Syro-Malabar parishes the morning brings the blessing of new fire and new water, the renewal of baptismal promises and the Holy Qurbana; the Resurrection service (Uyirppu) is held late tonight or before dawn on Sunday. Follow the timetable of your parish. From Easter until Pentecost the ‘Queen of Heaven’ (Regina Caeli) replaces the Angelus.
2027-03-27.verse: Therefore we have been buried with him by baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life.
theo: Great Saturday is the quietest day of the year. The body of the Lord lies in the new tomb in the garden, the stone is rolled across the door, and the disciples hide behind locked doors. Mary keeps watch in faith. Nothing seems to happen, and yet this is the day on which the Church confesses in the Creed: he descended into hell, among the dead. The First Letter of Peter says that Christ was “put to death in the flesh, but made alive in the spirit, in which also he went and made a proclamation to the spirits in prison” (1 Peter 3:18–19). An ancient homily for this day imagines the Lord going down to find Adam, taking him by the hand and saying: Awake, O sleeper, I did not make you to be held a prisoner in the underworld. The Saviour goes to the very bottom of human loss, so that no one, not even the dead of the ages before him, is beyond the reach of his rescue. The Church reads again the story of Abraham and Isaac, because Isaac was received back from the mountain as if from the dead; the Letter to the Hebrews says Abraham believed that God was able even to raise someone from the dead (Hebrews 11:17–19). The father who walked down Moriah with his living son is a first glimpse of the morning that is coming.

The second reading is the prayer of Jonah from the belly of the fish. Jonah had run from God and been thrown into the sea; now, from the depths, he prays: “I called to the LORD out of my distress, and he answered me; out of the belly of Sheol I cried, and you heard my voice.” He describes himself as already among the dead: “I went down to the land whose bars closed upon me forever; yet you brought up my life from the Pit, O LORD my God.” And then the strange and joyful ending: “Then the LORD spoke to the fish, and it spewed Jonah out upon the dry land.” Jesus himself chose this sign: “For just as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the sea monster, so for three days and three nights the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth” (Matthew 12:40). Jonah went down because of his disobedience; Jesus went down because of ours. Jonah came out to preach to Nineveh; the Risen One comes out to send his apostles to all the nations. The East Syriac tradition loves this sign: the Lord who was swallowed by death was, like Jonah, too much for death to keep.

Paul explains what this means for every baptised Christian. “Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? Therefore we have been buried with him by baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life.” Baptism is our own Great Saturday and our own Easter: the old self goes down into the water as into a tomb, and a new person rises. “We know that Christ, being raised from the dead, will never die again; death no longer has dominion over him.” That is why the ancient Church baptised on this night, and why the first week of Easter was the week of the newly baptised. Then the Gospel runs ahead of the clock: “After the sabbath, as the first day of the week was dawning”, the women come to the tomb, the earth shakes, an angel rolls back the stone and sits on it, and says: “Do not be afraid; I know that you are looking for Jesus who was crucified. He is not here; for he has been raised, as he said.” The Risen Lord meets the women on the road, and at the end he sends the eleven from a mountain in Galilee: “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit… And remember, I am with you always, to the end of the age.” The great silence of Saturday is the silence before the shout.

How a family can keep Great Saturday, step by step (the order and hours differ between dioceses and parishes; follow your own parish). First, the morning: in many parishes the faithful gather for the blessing of new fire and new water. The new fire speaks of Christ the light who cannot be put out; the blessed water speaks of Baptism. The people then renew their baptismal promises: they renounce Satan and all his works, and profess faith in the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. The Holy Qurbana follows in many places, and families carry the blessed water home to bless the house and the sick. Second, the day: the church stays quiet, and the faithful visit the tomb where the Lord's image lies. At home the house is cleaned and the Easter meal is prepared, but without noise: it is still a day of waiting, and many continue the fast until the Easter celebration. Third, the night: late on Saturday night or in the early hours of Sunday, the parish gathers in the dark for the Resurrection service (Uyirppu). The priest proclaims that Christ is risen, the church is filled with light, the bells ring out, the image of the Risen Lord is lifted up and carried in procession with candles, and the Holy Qurbana of the Resurrection is celebrated. Fourth, the return home: in many Kerala homes the fifty days of the Great Fast are broken only after this Qurbana, with appam and stew shared in joy. A good habit for today: let each person in the family find the date of his or her baptism, and thank God for it before going to the church tonight.
conn: Isaac received back.
Abraham “considered the fact that God is able even to raise someone from the dead”, and figuratively received Isaac back (Hebrews 11:19); the Father receives his Son back from the tomb.
The sign of Jonah.
Jonah's three days in the fish (Jonah 1:17) are the sign Jesus gives of his burial and Resurrection (Matthew 12:40).
The descent among the dead.
Christ “made a proclamation to the spirits in prison” (1 Peter 3:19); “the gospel was proclaimed even to the dead” (1 Peter 4:6).
The sabbath rest.
On the seventh day God rested from all his work (Genesis 2:2); on the seventh day the Son rests in the tomb, his work of redemption finished.
The flood and the water.
Noah's family was saved through water, and Peter writes: “And baptism, which this prefigured, now saves you” (1 Peter 3:20–21).
The Great Commission.
The Gospel ends with the command to baptise all nations (Matthew 28:19); the first sermon of Peter ends the same way (Acts 2:38).
altar: Every Holy Qurbana proclaims the death of the Lord and his Resurrection together. The Body laid in the tomb is the Body that rose, and it is this living, risen Body that we receive at the altar.
The baptismal promises renewed today are renewed at every Qurbana: we come to the altar as people who have died to sin with Christ and live for God in him.
outline: Opening
The great silence: the Lord rests in the tomb.
Point 1 · Isaac received back
Moriah and the hope of resurrection.
Point 2 · The sign of Jonah
From the belly of Sheol, a voice that God hears.
Point 3 · Buried with him in Baptism
The old self in the tomb, the new self rising.
Point 4 · He is not here
The stone rolled back and the sending to all nations.
Closing image
A dark church before dawn, one flame passed from candle to candle until every face is lit.
Take-home line
“He is not here; for he has been raised, as he said.”
live: Find your baptism date
Ask your parents or the parish register for the date of your baptism, and thank God for it today.
Renew your promises
Take part in the renewal of baptismal promises, or say the Creed slowly at home with your family.
Keep the waiting
Visit the tomb in the church and keep part of the day quiet, without noise or parties.
Go to the Uyirppu
Bring the whole family to the Resurrection service tonight or before dawn, even the sleepy children.
fathers: An ancient homily for Holy Saturday (in substance)

Something strange is happening: a great silence on earth, because the King is asleep. God has died in the flesh and gone to rouse those who have slept since the world began. He takes Adam by the hand and says: Awake, O sleeper, and rise from the dead; I am your God, who for your sake became your son. I did not create you to be held a prisoner in the underworld.
St Ephrem the Syrian (in substance)

Our Lord was trodden down by death, and in turn he trod out a way over death. Death slew him by means of the body that he had put on, but that same body proved to be the weapon by which he conquered death. Death could not devour him; it was forced to give him up, and all the dead with him.
magis: Catechism 631–635
Christ descended into the realm of the dead as Saviour, proclaiming the Good News to the spirits imprisoned there; this is the last phase of his messianic mission.
Catechism 624–627
Christ's stay in the tomb is the real link between his state before and after Easter; his body did not see corruption.
Catechism 1214–1215
Baptism means to plunge or immerse: a burial into Christ's death from which one rises by resurrection with him.
Catechism 1217–1222
The Church sees the great figures of Baptism in creation, the flood, the crossing of the sea and the Jordan.
Catechism 628
Baptism signifies efficaciously the descent into the tomb of the Christian who dies to sin with Christ in order to live a new life.
saints: Easter

Sunday 28 March: the Resurrection of our Lord (Uyirppu). Friday 2 April: in the East Syriac tradition, the first Friday after Easter is the feast of all the saints (verify locally). Sunday 4 April: New Sunday (Puthu Njayar), the confession of St Thomas.
2027-03-27.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, today you rest in the tomb, and the whole earth keeps silence. You went down among the dead to seek Adam and all his children, and death could not hold you. We were buried with you in Baptism; raise us with you to newness of life. Keep us faithful in the waiting, like Mary your Mother, and let the light of your Resurrection fill our homes and our hearts. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.

2027-03-28.title: Easter Sunday: the Resurrection of our Lord (Uyirppu)
2027-03-28.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: The glory of God over Jerusalem
Hannah's song: rejoice in the Lord
2027-03-28.alt: Easter Sunday, the feast of feasts. The Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta) begins and lasts seven weeks, until Pentecost. The calendar lists two Gospel passages (Matthew 28:1–6 and John 20:1–18); verify locally which is read at the night service and which at the Qurbana of the day. The fifty days of the Great Fast end with the Resurrection Qurbana.
2027-03-28.verse: He is not here; for he has been raised, as he said. Come, see the place where he lay.
theo: “Arise, shine; for your light has come, and the glory of the LORD has risen upon you.” The first words the Church hears on Easter are a summons to a city sitting in darkness. Isaiah speaks to a Jerusalem that has been ruined and emptied: “For darkness shall cover the earth, and thick darkness the peoples; but the LORD will arise upon you, and his glory will appear over you. Nations shall come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your dawn.” The prophet sees sons and daughters coming home from far away, the wealth of the nations streaming in, camels from Midian and Sheba bringing gold and frankincense, flocks offered on God's altar. On Easter morning the prophecy finds its true meaning. The light that has come is not a sunrise over a city but a Person risen from the dead. The Syro-Malabar Church celebrates the Uyirppu in the night or before dawn precisely for this reason: the darkness of the church is broken by light, and the people who sat in the shadow of death see the glory of the Lord. Every candle in our hands this night is a small fulfilment of Isaiah: nations coming to the light, and the sons and daughters of the Church gathered from everywhere, from Kerala to the farthest diaspora, singing the same Alleluia.

Then the Church sings with Hannah. She was the barren wife who wept in the temple, mocked by her rival, misunderstood even by the priest. God gave her a son, Samuel, and she poured out her joy: “My heart exults in the LORD; my strength is exalted in my God.” Her song is a song of reversals: the bows of the mighty are broken, the hungry are fed, the barren woman bears seven. And at its centre is a line that only Easter fully explains: “The LORD kills and brings to life; he brings down to Sheol and raises up.” “He raises up the poor from the dust; he lifts the needy from the ash heap, to make them sit with princes.” Mary of Nazareth would echo this song in her Magnificat. On Easter God does the greatest reversal of all: the one who was condemned is vindicated, the one laid in the dust of the tomb is raised, the crucified is made Lord. Paul draws the consequence for us: we who were baptised into his death are to live as people raised from the dead. “So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus.” “No longer present your members to sin as instruments of wickedness, but present yourselves to God as those who have been brought from death to life.” “For sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace.” Easter is not only something that happened to Jesus; it is something that has happened to us.

The Gospels tell the morning in two voices. In Matthew the women come to see the tomb; there is a great earthquake; an angel rolls back the stone and sits on it, and the guards become like dead men. The angel says: “Do not be afraid; I know that you are looking for Jesus who was crucified. He is not here; for he has been raised, as he said. Come, see the place where he lay.” In John it is still dark when Mary Magdalene comes and finds the stone removed. She runs to Peter and the beloved disciple; they race to the tomb, and the other disciple “saw and believed”, though he saw only the linen wrappings lying there and the cloth rolled up in a place by itself. Then the most tender scene of all. Mary stays outside weeping. She does not recognise Jesus and thinks he is the gardener. He calls her by name: “Mary!” And she turns and says, “Rabbouni!” The Risen Lord is not a ghost or a memory or an idea; he is the same Jesus who knows his own by name, risen in his own body, the body that bore the wounds. He sends her as the first messenger of Easter: “Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, ‘I have seen the Lord’.” The Church has called her the apostle to the apostles. The Resurrection is a real event in history, witnessed by many: an empty tomb, a stone rolled away, and above all meetings with the living Lord. It is also more than history: Christ has passed through death into a new life in which he will never die again, and he draws us with him.

How a family can follow the Uyirppu, step by step (the order and hours differ between dioceses; follow your parish). First, the gathering in darkness: late on Saturday night or in the early hours of Sunday the people gather in the church, often with the lights off, holding unlit candles. Second, the proclamation: the priest announces the Resurrection of the Lord. In many parishes the curtain is drawn back or the image of the Risen Christ is lifted from the tomb where the crucified Lord was laid on Friday, and the light spreads from candle to candle until the whole church shines. Third, the bells and the hymn of glory: the bells, silent since Pesaha, ring out, and the people sing the hymns of the Resurrection. Fourth, the procession: the image of the Risen Lord is carried around the church with candles, crosses and umbrellas, and the people follow singing; in some places it is accompanied by the joyful sound of bells and fireworks. Fifth, the Holy Qurbana of the Resurrection, the first Qurbana of Easter, in which we receive the living Body of the risen Lord. Sixth, the greeting and the meal: people greet one another with the Easter joy, and families go home to break the fifty days' fast together, often with appam and stew or meat curry, and to share with the poor. The fast was never an end in itself; its whole purpose was to bring us here, to the empty tomb and the living Lord. A practical word: take a moment at home to bless the table with the water blessed on Great Saturday, and let the head of the family say: Christ is risen. And let all answer: He is truly risen.
conn: The light over Jerusalem.

“Arise, shine; for your light has come” (Isaiah 60:1); Christ says, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12), and the women come to the tomb “as the first day of the week was dawning” (Matthew 28:1).
Hannah and Mary.
Hannah's song (1 Samuel 2:1–10) is echoed in Mary's Magnificat (Luke 1:46–55); both sing of a God who lifts up the lowly. At Easter he lifts up his Son from the dust of death.
The garden.
