Adam and Eve lost life in a garden (Genesis 3:23–24); Jesus is buried and rises in a garden (John 19:41), and Mary thinks he is the gardener (John 20:15).
Called by name.
“I have called you by name, you are mine” (Isaiah 43:1); the good shepherd “calls his own sheep by name” (John 10:3), and Mary knows him when he says “Mary!” (John 20:16).
The sign of Jonah fulfilled.
Jesus promised the sign of Jonah (Matthew 12:40); “on the third day” he is raised, “in accordance with the scriptures” (1 Corinthians 15:4).
The day the LORD has made.
“This is the day that the LORD has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it” (Psalm 118:24): the psalm of the rejected stone becomes the song of Easter.
altar: The Resurrection is the heart of the Holy Qurbana. We do not receive a dead memory but the living Lord, his true Body and Blood, risen and glorified. The Qurbana is the Easter meal of the Church, celebrated every Sunday because every Sunday is a little Easter.
As Mary Magdalene was called by name at the tomb, so each of us is called by name at the altar to receive the Body of Christ. The Amen we say at Communion is our ‘Rabbouni’.
outline: Opening
Darkness, a single flame, and the cry: Christ is risen!
Point 1 · Arise, shine
Isaiah's light and the night of the Uyirppu.
Point 2 · He raises up the poor from the dust
Hannah's song of reversals.
Point 3 · Dead to sin, alive to God
What Easter does to the baptised.
Point 4 · Mary!
The empty tomb and the Lord who calls us by name.
Closing image
A woman weeping in a garden turns at the sound of her own name, and sees the Lord.
Take-home line
“He is not here; for he has been raised, as he said.”
live: Greet with the news
Greet every family member and friend today with the words: Christ is risen!
Break the fast together
Share the Easter meal with the whole family, and invite or send food to someone who is alone.
Live as risen
Choose one sin you will no longer ‘present your members’ to, and replace it with a work of grace (Romans 6:13).
Keep the fifty days
Make Easter last: pray the ‘Queen of Heaven’ (Regina Caeli) at noon each day until Pentecost.
fathers: St John Chrysostom, Paschal homily (in substance)

Let no one fear death, for the death of the Saviour has set us free. He has destroyed it by enduring it. Hell took a body and met God face to face; it took earth and encountered heaven. O death, where is your sting? O hell, where is your victory? Christ is risen, and you are overthrown; Christ is risen, and life reigns.
St Ephrem the Syrian (in substance)

Blessed is he who was crucified, who came down from the Cross and went down to Sheol, and rose and gathered us into his Church. The dead heard his voice in Sheol, and Sheol vomited them out, as the sea gave back Jonah. Glory to the Hidden One who became visible, and to the Dead One who came to life.
magis: Catechism 638–639
The Resurrection of Jesus is the crowning truth of our faith; it is a real event with historically verifiable manifestations.
Catechism 640
The empty tomb is the first step towards recognising the Resurrection; it is not in itself a direct proof.
Catechism 645–646
The risen Jesus is the same one who suffered; his body is real but glorified, no longer bound to space and time. The Resurrection is not a return to earthly life.
Catechism 654–655
The Resurrection opens for us the way to a new life: justification restores us to God's grace, and Christ is the principle and source of our future resurrection.
Catechism 1169
Easter is not simply one feast among others but the Feast of feasts.
saints: Easter week

Monday 29 March to Saturday 3 April: the first week of Resurrection, the week of the newly baptised. Friday 2 April: in the East Syriac tradition, the feast of all the saints (verify locally). Sunday 4 April: New Sunday (Puthu Njayar), the confession of St Thomas: “My Lord and my God!” The Annunciation, which fell on Pesaha this year, is kept as the Syro-Malabar Ordo directs (verify locally).
2027-03-28.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you are risen from the dead, and death no longer has dominion over you. Glory to you! You broke the bars of Sheol, you rolled away the stone, and you called Mary by her name in the garden. Call us by name, too, and turn our weeping into joy. Make us dead to sin and alive to God; let us walk in newness of life as children of the light. Fill your Church in every land with the gladness of this day, and bring us at last, with all the saints, to the feast that has no end. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen. Alleluia!

2027-03-01.title: Fourth Monday of the Great Fast
2027-03-01.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: The healing at the pool of Beth-zatha
2027-03-01.alt: Season of the Great Fast (Sauma Ramba).
2027-03-01.verse: When Jesus saw him lying there and knew that he had been there a long time, he said to him, “Do you want to be made well?”
theo: The fourth week of the Great Fast opens with a journey. God speaks to a man of seventy-five who has every reason to stay where he is: “Go from your country and your kindred and your father's house to the land that I will show you.” The promise is enormous, “I will make of you a great nation, and I will bless you, and make your name great, so that you will be a blessing”, but the map is blank. And the most important sentence in the reading is the shortest: “So Abram went, as the LORD had told him.” Notice what Abram does at every stop. At Shechem “he built there an altar to the LORD”, and near Bethel he pitched his tent “and there he built an altar to the LORD and invoked the name of the LORD.” Wherever his tent goes, an altar goes with it. The Syro-Malabar families who left Travancore in the last century to clear the forests of Malabar and the high ranges did the same: before the houses had proper roofs there was a small chapel, and the Holy Qurbana was offered among the stumps and the new rubber. The Great Fast asks each of us where God is asking us to go, and whether our tent still has an altar beside it.

Last Sunday we heard that one man had hidden plunder in his tent and that all Israel was weakened by it. Today the hidden thing comes out. Tribe by tribe, clan by clan, household by household, the lot narrows until Achan stands alone. Joshua's words to him are surprisingly gentle: “My son, give glory to the LORD God of Israel and make confession to him. Tell me now what you have done; do not hide it from me.” Achan answers: “It is true; I am the one who sinned against the LORD God of Israel.” The ending of this ancient story is grim, and the place is named the Valley of Achor, the valley of trouble. But the prophets did not leave it there. Through Hosea God promised to “make the Valley of Achor a door of hope” (Hosea 2:15). In the Church of Christ that promise is kept every time a sinner kneels in confession: the valley of trouble becomes a door of hope, and the one who says “I am the one who sinned” goes home forgiven.

Paul begins the great chapters of Romans on Israel with tears: “I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart.” He loves his own people, and he lists their gifts with pride: “to them belong the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the worship, and the promises; to them belong the patriarchs, and from them, according to the flesh, comes the Messiah.” The Church has learned from him to speak of the Jewish people with reverence, never with contempt. In the Gospel Jesus goes to a pool where the sick lay waiting for the water to be stirred. One man had been ill “for thirty-eight years.” Jesus asks him what sounds like a strange question: “Do you want to be made well?” The man does not say yes; he explains why it has never worked: “Sir, I have no one to put me into the pool when the water is stirred up.” Jesus does not need the pool. “Stand up, take your mat and walk.” Later he finds the man in the temple and adds: “See, you have been made well! Do not sin any more, so that nothing worse happens to you.” When John writes that “the Jews” began to persecute Jesus, he means certain religious authorities in Jerusalem, not the Jewish people as a whole, for Jesus, his mother and all his apostles were Jews (Catechism 597). Halfway through the fast, the same question is put to us: do you want to be made well, or only to explain why you are still lying by the pool?
outline: Opening
Ask: do I want to be made well, or do I prefer my explanations?
Point 1 · So Abram went
A journey with an altar at every stop.
Point 2 · Make confession
Achan's valley of trouble and the door of hope.
Point 3 · Stand up and walk
Thirty-eight years by the pool, and one word from Jesus.
Take-home line
“Do you want to be made well?”
live: Answer the question (John 5:6)
Name one sin or habit you have lived with for a long time, and bring it to confession before Palm Sunday.
Keep an altar beside the tent
Wherever you are this week, at home, in a hostel or abroad, set apart one corner and one fixed time for prayer.
2027-03-01.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you saw the man lying by the pool and knew how long he had waited. Look on us too, and ask us again whether we want to be made well. Give us the faith of Abram to go where you send us, the honesty of a sinner who confesses, and the courage to stand up and walk. Turn every valley of trouble in our lives into a door of hope. Amen.
altar: The Holy Qurbana is the altar Abram carried in hope: wherever the Church pitches her tent, the Son offers himself to the Father, and the sick are told once more, “Stand up, take your mat and walk.”

2027-03-02.title: Fourth Tuesday of the Great Fast
2027-03-02.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: That all may honour the Son
2027-03-02.alt: Season of the Great Fast (Sauma Ramba).
2027-03-02.verse: So it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God who shows mercy.
theo: Yesterday Abram set out in faith; today, a few verses later, he is afraid. “Now there was a famine in the land. So Abram went down to Egypt to reside there as an alien.” At the border he makes a plan to save his own skin: “Say you are my sister, so that it may go well with me because of you, and that my life may be spared on your account.” The father of faith tells a half-lie, and Sarai pays for it: she is taken into Pharaoh's house. It is the pagan king who has to rebuke the man of God: “What is this you have done to me? Why did you not tell me that she was your wife?” Scripture does not polish its heroes. Faith is not a straight line from call to glory; it stumbles, it is afraid, it uses others to protect itself. And yet God does not abandon the promise or the woman who carries it: “the LORD afflicted Pharaoh and his house with great plagues because of Sarai, Abram's wife.” There is a word here for every marriage. Fear can make a husband or a wife sacrifice the other to save themselves; God stands on the side of the one who is sacrificed.

The second reading follows the confession of Achan. Israel had been routed at Ai; now the sin has been brought into the light, and God speaks again: “Do not fear or be dismayed; take all the fighting men with you, and go up now to Ai.” The place of defeat becomes the place of a new beginning. These battle stories belong to a hard and ancient world, and the Church does not read them as a pattern for treating any people; the Fathers read them as pictures of our own struggle against sin. Read that way, the lesson is clear and consoling. After a fall and a good confession, God does not send us somewhere easier. He sends us back to the same Ai, the same temptation, the same weak place, but now he goes with us.

Paul faces a hard question: if God chooses, is God unjust? “By no means!” he answers, and quotes the word God spoke to Moses: “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion.” Then comes the sentence that stands over the whole Great Fast: “So it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God who shows mercy.” Our fasting is not wasted effort, but it is not a payment either. We fast to make room for a mercy we could never earn. In the Gospel Jesus reveals where that mercy comes from: “the Son can do nothing on his own, but only what he sees the Father doing; for whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise.” The Father “loves the Son and shows him all that he himself is doing”, and has given him the power to give life and to judge, “so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father.” This is the faith of the Church: Jesus is not merely a good teacher but the eternal Son, one with the Father. That is why, at the Holy Qurbana, we bow before him and adore.
outline: Opening
Ask: when I am afraid, whom do I sacrifice to save myself?
Point 1 · Say you are my sister
The father of faith afraid in Egypt.
Point 2 · Go up now to Ai
Back to the place of defeat, with God.
Point 3 · God who shows mercy
Not exertion but mercy, revealed in the Son.
Take-home line
“It depends not on human will or exertion, but on God who shows mercy.”
live: Tell the truth (Ephesians 4:25)
Correct one half-truth you have told, at home or at work, before the week is out.
Go back to Ai
Identify the place where you usually fall, and plan with God one concrete change for that place.
2027-03-02.prayer: Merciful Father, Abram was afraid and you kept your promise; Israel was defeated and you sent them out again. Do not look on our fears and our half-truths, but on your mercy. Teach us to honour your Son as we honour you, and to do what we see him doing. Lead us back to the places where we fell, and walk there with us. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana we honour the Son as we honour the Father: we adore him present on the altar, and receive from him the life the Father has given him to give.

2027-03-03.title: Fourth Wednesday of the Great Fast · Mid-Lent
2027-03-03.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: You have the words of eternal life
2027-03-03.alt: Season of the Great Fast (Sauma Ramba). Mid-Lent: the Great Fast reaches its midpoint today. In some parishes the Cross is honoured with special prayers; follow local custom.
2027-03-03.verse: Simon Peter answered him, “Lord, to whom can we go? You have the words of eternal life.
theo: Today the Great Fast reaches its midpoint. The calendar marks this Wednesday as Mid-Lent: as many days lie behind us as before us, and the Resurrection is now nearer than Ash Monday. It is a good day to stop, look back honestly, and begin again. The first reading shows a quarrel that every Kerala family knows. Abram and his nephew Lot have grown rich, “and there was strife between the herders of Abram's livestock and the herders of Lot's livestock.” Abram is the elder; by custom he could choose first. Instead he says: “Let there be no strife between you and me, and between your herders and my herders; for we are kindred. Is not the whole land before you?” Lot looks with his eyes and chooses the best: the plain of the Jordan, “well watered everywhere like the garden of the LORD”, and he moves his tent “as far as Sodom.” Then, when Abram has let go, God speaks: “Raise your eyes now, and look from the place where you are, northward and southward and eastward and westward; for all the land that you see I will give to you and to your offspring forever.” The man who gave up the first choice receives everything. Many of our families carry wounds from partitions of land and houses, brothers who have not spoken for years over a boundary stone. Mid-Lent is a good day to say Abram's sentence: we are kindred.

The second reading tells of the fall of Ai. God says to Joshua: “Stretch out the sword that is in your hand toward Ai; for I will give it into your hand.” Joshua does not lower his hand until the battle is over, and the king of Ai is hanged on a tree until evening and taken down at sunset. It is a fierce story from a fierce age. Origen, preaching on this chapter, read it in the light of the Cross (in substance): the outstretched hand of Joshua, whose name is the same as the name of Jesus, points to the arms of Christ stretched out on the wood, and the enemy hanged on the tree points to the powers of evil that Christ disarmed on the Cross, “triumphing over them in it” (Colossians 2:15). At the middle of the fast the Church holds up the Cross before us: the battle is not ours alone, and it has already been won.

Paul longs for the salvation of his people, who have “a zeal for God”, and he shows how near salvation is: “The word is near you, on your lips and in your heart”; “if you confess with your lips that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.” And it is for all: “Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved.” The Gospel takes us to the end of the great sermon on the Bread of Life. Jesus has said that his flesh is true food and his blood true drink, and many disciples say: “This teaching is difficult; who can accept it?” They do not misunderstand him; they understand him and leave. “Because of this many of his disciples turned back and no longer went about with him.” Jesus does not soften his words or call them back with a gentler explanation. He turns to the Twelve: “Do you also wish to go away?” Peter answers for the Church of every age: “Lord, to whom can we go? You have the words of eternal life. We have come to believe and know that you are the Holy One of God.” At the midpoint of the fast, some of us are tired, and some have quietly given up. Jesus asks the same question. Peter's answer is still the only one that makes sense.
outline: Opening
Mid-Lent: look back honestly, and begin again.
Point 1 · We are kindred
Abram lets go, and receives everything.
Point 2 · The outstretched hand
The Cross held up at the middle of the fast.
Point 3 · To whom can we go?
The hard teaching of the Bread of Life, and Peter's answer.
Take-home line
“Lord, to whom can we go? You have the words of eternal life.”
live: Make peace (Genesis 13:8)
If there is a quarrel over property or inheritance in your family, take one step toward peace before Palm Sunday.
Renew the fast
Look back over the first half of the fast; take up again one resolution you have dropped, and add a visit to the Blessed Sacrament this week.
2027-03-03.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, at the middle of the fast you ask us whether we too wish to go away. We answer with Peter: to whom can we go? You have the words of eternal life. Give us the generosity of Abram to let go for the sake of peace, the faith to confess you with our lips and believe in our hearts, and the strength to walk the rest of the way to your Cross and Resurrection. Amen.
altar: The teaching that made many disciples leave is the gift we receive at every Holy Qurbana: the flesh of the Son of Man given for the life of the world. We stay, because he has the words of eternal life.

2027-03-04.title: Fourth Thursday of the Great Fast
2027-03-04.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
2027-03-04.alt: Season of the Great Fast (Sauma Ramba). In the Latin calendar, St Casimir is commemorated today.
2027-03-04.verse: God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew.
theo: Lot had chosen the well-watered plain and moved his tent toward Sodom. Now the kings of the region go to war, Sodom is plundered, and “they also took Lot, the son of Abram's brother, who lived in Sodom, and his goods, and departed.” Abram could have said: he chose it; let him live with it. Instead, “When Abram heard that his nephew had been taken captive, he led forth his trained men, born in his house, three hundred eighteen of them, and went in pursuit as far as Dan.” He fights by night, routs the raiders, and “brought back his nephew Lot with his goods, and the women and the people.” This is the love that goes after the one who walked away. Many of us have a Lot in the family: a son who chose another road, a sister who moved far from the faith, a relative who is now caught in debt or drink. The Great Fast asks us not to say “he chose it” but to go after them with prayer, patience and practical help. In the verses that follow, Melchizedek, priest of God Most High, comes out to meet Abram with bread and wine (Genesis 14:18). The Letter to the Hebrews sees in him a figure of Christ the eternal priest, and the Church sees in his offering a figure of the bread and wine of the Holy Qurbana.

After the victory at Ai, Joshua does something unexpected: he stops to worship. He builds on Mount Ebal “an altar of unhewn stones, on which no iron tool has been used”, offers sacrifices, writes the law on stones, and then reads it aloud. “There was not a word of all that Moses commanded that Joshua did not read before all the assembly of Israel, and the women, and the little ones, and the aliens who resided among them.” Word and altar, everyone gathered, no one left out: this is the shape of every Holy Qurbana. First the word of God is proclaimed to the whole assembly, then the offering is made on the altar. And notice who is there: women, little ones and strangers. Children belong at the Holy Qurbana, not only when they behave; and the readings belong to them too, if parents take a minute on the way home to ask what they heard.

Paul asks the question many Christians have asked carelessly: “has God rejected his people? By no means!” He answers as an Israelite himself: “God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew.” When Elijah complained that he alone was left, God answered: “I have kept for myself seven thousand who have not bowed the knee to Baal.” “So too at the present time there is a remnant, chosen by grace.” The Second Vatican Council, drawing on these chapters, taught that the Jews remain most dear to God for the sake of their fathers, for God does not take back his gifts or his call (Nostra Aetate 4). Elijah's complaint is also our temptation: to think we are the only faithful ones left. God always has his seven thousand. In the Gospel the festival of Booths is near, the great autumn feast when Israel lived in shelters to remember the desert. Jesus' relatives urge him to go up and make a name: “no one who wants to be widely known acts in secret.” John adds sadly: “(For not even his brothers believed in him.)” Jesus answers: “My time has not yet come”, and later goes up “not publicly but as it were in secret.” The crowds argue about him, but no one speaks openly “for fear of the Jews”, which in John means fear of certain authorities, since the crowds themselves were Jews. Jesus does not follow the timetable of publicity. He waits for the Father's hour, and in this fast he teaches us to do our good works in secret too.
outline: Opening
Ask: who is the Lot in my family, and have I gone after him?
Point 1 · He went in pursuit
Abram rescues the one who chose another road.
Point 2 · Word and altar
Joshua reads the law to all, women, children and strangers.
Point 3 · Not rejected
A remnant chosen by grace, and Jesus who waits for the Father's hour.
Take-home line
“God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew.”
live: Go after one (Genesis 14:14)
Phone, visit or write to one relative or friend who has drifted away, without lecturing; simply show that you care.
Bring the children
Take the children to the Holy Qurbana this week and on the way home ask each one what they heard in the readings.
2027-03-04.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you went after us when we had chosen the road to Sodom, and you brought us back. Give us the heart of Abram for those who have strayed, the faith of Joshua who gathered all the people around the word and the altar, and the patience to wait for the Father's hour. Keep us from thinking we alone are faithful, and bless the people of the first covenant, whom you have never rejected. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana, as at Mount Ebal, the whole people gathers: the word is read to all, and the offering is made on the altar. Melchizedek's bread and wine find their fulfilment in the Body and Blood of Christ, the eternal priest.

2027-03-05.title: Fourth Friday of the Great Fast · First Friday
2027-03-05.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: God makes a covenant with Abram
The depth of the riches of God
2027-03-05.alt: Season of the Great Fast (Sauma Ramba). First Friday of the month: devotion to the Sacred Heart, confession and Holy Qurbana. A Friday of abstinence from meat; the Way of the Cross is prayed in parishes and homes.
2027-03-05.verse: And he believed the LORD; and the LORD reckoned it to him as righteousness.
theo: Abram has left everything and has just risked his life to rescue Lot, but he is still childless, and he is tired. God comes to him in a vision: “Do not be afraid, Abram, I am your shield; your reward shall be very great.” Abram answers honestly, almost bitterly: “O Lord GOD, what will you give me, for I continue childless?” God does not scold him. “He brought him outside and said, ‘Look toward heaven and count the stars, if you are able to count them.’ Then he said to him, ‘So shall your descendants be.’” Nothing has changed outside; the tent is still empty of children. But something changes inside: “And he believed the LORD; and the LORD reckoned it to him as righteousness.” Then comes a strange and solemn rite. Abram cuts animals in two and lays the halves opposite each other. In the ancient world, the parties to a covenant walked between such pieces, as if to say: may I be torn like these if I break my word. But when darkness falls, only one passes through: “a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch passed between these pieces.” God alone walks the path; God alone binds himself. On a Friday the Church remembers how far that binding went: on the Cross God kept his covenant at the cost of his own Son's body, and Jesus could say of the cup, “the new covenant in my blood” (Luke 22:20).

The second reading is a story of clever deception. The people of Gibeon, a city close by, fear the fate of Jericho and Ai, so they dress in worn-out clothes and patched sandals, pack dry and mouldy bread, and arrive at Joshua's camp saying, “We have come from a far country; so now make a treaty with us.” The mouldy bread is convincing, and Israel signs. The sacred writer puts his finger on the real mistake: “So the leaders partook of their provisions, and did not ask direction from the LORD.” They used their eyes, their reason and their experience, and they forgot to pray. Many of our worst decisions, about marriage proposals, land deals, jobs abroad or business partners, are made the same way: we examine the bread and forget to ask the Lord. The First Friday is a good day to bring the decisions in front of us to the Heart of Jesus before we sign.

Paul ends his long meditation on Israel with a mystery: “a hardening has come upon part of Israel, until the full number of the Gentiles has come in. And so all Israel will be saved.” He insists that “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable”, and that “God has imprisoned all in disobedience so that he may be merciful to all.” Then he can only break into praise: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!” In the Gospel the people of Jerusalem argue about Jesus: “we know where this man is from.” Jesus cries out in the temple: “I have not come on my own. But the one who sent me is true, and you do not know him. I know him, because I am from him, and he sent me.” They try to arrest him, “but no one laid hands on him, because his hour had not yet come.” That hour would come on a Friday. On the Cross a soldier “pierced his side with a spear, and at once blood and water came out” (John 19:34). The First Friday devotion to the Sacred Heart, so loved in Kerala homes with the picture of the Heart above the family altar, is simply this: to look at the pierced side of the one God sent, and to see there how far the covenant goes.
outline: Opening
First Friday: look at the pierced Heart, and see how far God's covenant goes.
Point 1 · Count the stars
Abram believes when nothing has changed outside.
Point 2 · The fire between the pieces
God alone binds himself, all the way to the Cross.
Point 3 · They did not ask the Lord
Decisions made by examining the bread.
Point 4 · The depth of the riches
God's irrevocable call, and the hour that came on Friday.
Take-home line
“And he believed the LORD; and the LORD reckoned it to him as righteousness.”
live: Keep the First Friday
Go to confession and receive Holy Qurbana today if you can, and renew the consecration of your family to the Sacred Heart before the picture at home.
Ask before you sign (Joshua 9:14)
Bring one decision you are facing to prayer before the Blessed Sacrament before you act on it.
2027-03-05.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, sent by the Father, on the Cross your side was pierced and your Heart was opened for us. You are the fire that passed alone between the pieces, binding yourself to us for ever. Give us Abram's faith to believe when nothing has changed, the humility to ask your direction before we decide, and a heart that praises the depth of your riches. Sacred Heart of Jesus, we place all our trust in you. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the cup of the new covenant is offered: the blood that flowed from the pierced Heart, the covenant God sealed alone and keeps for ever.

2027-03-06.title: Fourth Saturday of the Great Fast
2027-03-06.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Never has anyone spoken like this
2027-03-06.alt: Season of the Great Fast (Sauma Ramba).
2027-03-06.verse: The police answered, “Never has anyone spoken like this!”
theo: Paul writes to Christians living in the capital of the empire, under rulers who were not Christian and not always just: “Let every person be subject to the governing authorities; for there is no authority except from God, and those authorities that exist have been instituted by God.” He is not flattering the emperor. He is saying that ordered government, which protects the weak and restrains the violent, is part of God's providence, and that the ruler is meant to be “God's servant for your good.” So Christians pay their taxes honestly, give respect and honour where they are due, and obey “not only because of wrath but also because of conscience.” Elsewhere the Church learned the limit of this obedience from the apostles themselves: when the authorities forbade them to preach Christ, Peter answered, “We must obey God rather than any human authority” (Acts 5:29). Jesus had already drawn the line: “Give therefore to the emperor the things that are the emperor's, and to God the things that are God's” (Matthew 22:21). The St Thomas Christians lived this balance for centuries under Hindu kings. The Tharisappalli copper plates of 849 record the privileges granted to the Christian community of Quilon by a local ruler, and our forefathers were known as loyal subjects and honest traders. A Christian citizen today pays tax without cheating, does not bribe, votes with conscience, prays for those in authority, and refuses only what is against God.

In the Gospel the chief priests and Pharisees had sent temple police to arrest Jesus. The police come back empty-handed. “Why did you not arrest him?” Their answer is one of the simplest confessions in the Gospel: “Never has anyone spoken like this!” They were not theologians; they had only listened. Their superiors are angry: “Surely you have not been deceived too, have you? Has any one of the authorities or of the Pharisees believed in him?” Then one voice rises in the council. Nicodemus, “who had gone to Jesus before, and who was one of them”, asks a careful question: “Our law does not judge people without first giving them a hearing to find out what they are doing, does it?” It is not yet a bold confession, only a plea for fairness, and he is mocked for it: “Surely you are not also from Galilee, are you?” But this small courage grows. On Good Friday the same Nicodemus will come openly to the Cross, “bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, weighing about a hundred pounds” (John 19:39), to bury the Lord. The Passion is drawing near. In families, parishes and offices, someone is always being condemned without a hearing. The Great Fast asks us for the courage of Nicodemus: to say, quietly and clearly, let us first hear him.
outline: Opening
Ask: am I an honest citizen and a fair judge?
Point 1 · Authority from God
Taxes, respect and conscience, and the limit: God first.
Point 2 · Never has anyone spoken like this
The police who only listened.
Point 3 · Give him a hearing
Nicodemus' small courage that grew.
Take-home line
“Never has anyone spoken like this!”
live: Be an honest citizen (Romans 13:7)
Check that your taxes, bills and documents are honest, and refuse any bribe this week, given or taken.
Speak like Nicodemus (John 7:51)
When someone is being criticised in their absence, say: let us first hear their side.
2027-03-06.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, the guards who came to arrest you went away saying: never has anyone spoken like this. Give us ears to listen to your word, honest hands in our duties as citizens, and the courage of Nicodemus to defend those who are condemned without a hearing. Bless all who govern, that they may serve the good of all, and keep us always faithful to God above every human power. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana we hear the voice of which the guards said, never has anyone spoken like this, and we receive the One whom Nicodemus buried and the Father raised.

2027-03-08.title: Fifth Monday of the Great Fast
2027-03-08.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Sell all and give to the poor
2027-03-08.alt: Season of the Great Fast (Sauma Ramba). The Latin Church commemorates St John of God today.
2027-03-08.verse: There is still one thing lacking. Sell all that you own and distribute the money to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me.
theo: The fifth week of the Great Fast opens with a warning that sounds, at first, almost against fasting. Some teachers in Colossae had turned religion into a matter of diet and calendar, of visions and the worship of angels, and they judged the believers who did not keep their rules. Paul writes: “Therefore do not let anyone condemn you in matters of food and drink or of observing festivals, new moons, or sabbaths. These are only a shadow of what is to come, but the substance belongs to Christ.” Paul does not despise fasting; the Church fasted from the beginning, and the St Thomas Christians have kept the fifty days of the Great Fast with great seriousness for centuries, giving up meat and fish, often eating one meal a day, sometimes sleeping on a mat on the floor. But every practice is a shadow, and a shadow is cast by something solid. The solid thing is Christ. A fast that makes me proud, or that makes me watch what my neighbour eats, has kept the shadow and lost the substance. Paul names the root of the trouble: such people are “not holding fast to the head, from whom the whole body, nourished and held together by its ligaments and sinews, grows with a growth that is from God.” The Great Fast is meant to bind us more closely to the Head and to one another, never to divide the body into the strict and the lax.

In the Gospel a ruler comes to Jesus with the deepest question a person can ask: “Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?” Jesus points him to the commandments, and the man answers honestly: “I have kept all these since my youth.” He is no hypocrite. He has kept the law, the shadow, faithfully. Then Jesus looks at him and says: “There is still one thing lacking. Sell all that you own and distribute the money to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me.” The one thing lacking is not one more rule. It is a Person: come, follow me. “But when he heard this, he became sad; for he was very rich.” Jesus does not run after him to lower the price. He says, with sorrow: “How hard it is for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God!” Not everyone is called to sell everything, as the apostles and the religious do; but everyone is asked what holds the heart. The Latin Church today remembers St John of God, a Portuguese soldier and bookseller who, after hearing a sermon in Granada, gave away his stock of books and spent the rest of his life carrying the sick poor into a house he opened for them. In many of our parishes the money saved by fasting is put into a Lenten box for the poor. It is a small way of hearing the same word: sell, give, come, follow.
outline: Opening
Ask: what is the one thing still lacking in me?
Point 1 · Shadow and substance
Fasting points to Christ and must never divide the body.
Point 2 · Kept since my youth
A good man who stopped one step short.
Point 3 · Come, follow me
Treasure in heaven and the eye of the needle.
Take-home line
“There is still one thing lacking.”
live: Fill the Lenten box (Luke 18:22)
Put into your parish's Lenten box, or give directly to someone in need, what your fasting has saved this week.
Do not judge another's fast (Colossians 2:16)
Today, say nothing about what others eat or do not eat, and let your own fast be known only to God.
2027-03-08.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you are the substance of every shadow and the treasure of every heart. Do not let our fasting make us proud or quick to judge, but bind us more closely to you, our Head, and to one another. Show us the one thing still lacking in us, and give us the courage not to go away sad, but to give, and to come, and to follow you. Through the prayers of St John of God, make us servants of the sick and the poor. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the shadow gives way to the substance: the bread and wine become the Body and Blood of Christ, and the Head nourishes the whole body that grows with a growth that is from God.

2027-03-09.title: Fifth Tuesday of the Great Fast
2027-03-09.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
2027-03-09.alt: Season of the Great Fast (Sauma Ramba). The Latin Church commemorates St Frances of Rome today.
theo: Paul is collecting money. For years he gathered a collection from the Gentile churches of Greece and Asia for the poor believers in Jerusalem, and in this chapter he encourages the Corinthians to finish what they had promised. He does not scold; he speaks of God as a farmer who supplies the farmer: “He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your seed for sowing and increase the harvest of your righteousness.” Giving is sowing, and God is the one who makes it grow. “You will be enriched in every way for your great generosity, which will produce thanksgiving to God through us.” What is remarkable is where Paul's eyes rest. The collection will feed the hungry, but it will do more: it will make the poor of Jerusalem give thanks to God, and pray for the Gentiles who once seemed strangers. The gift builds the one Church: “they long for you and pray for you because of the surpassing grace of God that he has given you.” And then, as if all talk of money had brought him to the greatest Gift of all, Paul breaks into praise: “Thanks be to God for his indescribable gift!” The Great Fast has always had three companions: prayer, fasting and almsgiving. Almsgiving here is not a tax paid to God, but seed sown in his field, which returns as thanksgiving and communion.

The Gospel takes us to the road from Jerusalem down to Jericho, a steep and lonely road where robbers waited. A man lies there half dead. A priest and a Levite pass by on the other side. “But a Samaritan while traveling came near him; and when he saw him, he was moved with pity.” Jesus' hearers did not expect the hero to be a Samaritan, a member of a people with whom they had long quarrelled. Everything the Samaritan does is concrete: “He went to him and bandaged his wounds, having poured oil and wine on them. Then he put him on his own animal, brought him to an inn, and took care of him.” He pays two denarii, about two days' wages, and promises more. The lawyer had asked, “who is my neighbor?”, a question about where to draw the line. Jesus turns it round: “Which of these three, do you think, was a neighbor to the man who fell into the hands of the robbers?” “The one who showed him mercy.” “Go and do likewise.” The Fathers saw Christ himself in the Samaritan, who came down to our road, poured the oil and wine of the sacraments on our wounds, and brought us to the inn of the Church. The Latin Church today remembers St Frances of Rome, a noblewoman, wife and mother who, through famine and plague, turned her family's house into a storehouse and hospital for the poor of Rome. She did not leave her home or her marriage to be a neighbour; she opened them.
outline: Opening
Ask: whose wounds have I passed by on the other side?
Point 1 · Seed for the sower
Almsgiving as sowing in God's field.
Point 2 · Moved with pity
The Samaritan who came near.
Point 3 · His indescribable gift
Mercy that ends in thanksgiving.
Take-home line
“Go and do likewise.”
live: Come near (Luke 10:34)
Visit, call or help one person this week whom you have been passing by: a lonely neighbour, a sick relative, a migrant worker.
Sow generously (2 Corinthians 9:10)
Decide on a definite Lenten alms and give it before Hosanna Sunday.
2027-03-09.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you came down to our road, saw us half dead, and were moved with pity. You poured oil and wine on our wounds and brought us to the inn of your Church. Make us neighbours to everyone we meet; open our hands to sow generously, and our lips to give thanks for your indescribable gift. Through the prayers of St Frances of Rome, make our homes places of mercy. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the Good Samaritan still comes near: he pours the oil and wine of his grace on our wounds, and gives himself, the indescribable gift, for which we give thanks.

2027-03-10.title: Fifth Wednesday of the Great Fast
2027-03-10.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: The end of those who walk away from God
2027-03-10.alt: Season of the Great Fast (Sauma Ramba).
2027-03-10.verse: Neither do I condemn you. Go your way, and from now on do not sin again.
theo: The little letter of Jude, tucked in just before the Book of Revelation, is one of the sternest pages of the New Testament. It was written against people inside the community who, Jude says, “defile the flesh, reject authority, and slander the glorious ones.” Yet in the middle of his rebuke he sets a strange example. Even the archangel Michael, when he “contended with the devil and disputed about the body of Moses, he did not dare to bring a condemnation of slander against him, but said, ‘The Lord rebuke you!’” If the greatest of the angels left judgment to God, how much more should we. Then Jude pours out images of a life that promises much and gives nothing: “These are blemishes on your love-feasts, while they feast with you without fear, feeding themselves. They are waterless clouds carried along by the winds; autumn trees without fruit, twice dead, uprooted.” In March, when the heat lies heavy on Kerala, farmers look up at every cloud that gathers over the hills, hoping for the first summer shower; a cloud that passes without a drop is a bitter thing. Jude names three old figures of the way away from God: Cain, who killed his brother in envy; Balaam, who sold his gift for gain; Korah, who rebelled against the order God had given. Envy, greed and pride are still the roads by which a believer becomes a waterless cloud. The Great Fast asks: when people come to me, do they find rain, or only shade that passes? And Jude's own letter does not end in condemnation; a few verses later he tells the faithful to have mercy on those who waver, and to snatch others out of the fire.

The Gospel shows us how Jesus judges. Early in the morning, as he sits teaching in the temple, some scribes and Pharisees bring a woman “who had been caught in adultery; and making her stand before all of them,” they say: “Teacher, this woman was caught in the very act of committing adultery. Now in the law Moses commanded us to stone such women. Now what do you say?” She is not a person to them but a trap; the man is nowhere to be seen. “Jesus bent down and wrote with his finger on the ground.” No one knows what he wrote; the Fathers remembered that the finger of God had once written the law on stone. When they press him, he stands and says: “Let anyone among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her.” And he bends down again. “When they heard it, they went away, one by one, beginning with the elders.” St Augustine said that in the end only two were left, misery and mercy (in substance). Then Jesus stands and speaks to her for the first time: “Woman, where are they? Has no one condemned you?” “No one, sir.” “Neither do I condemn you. Go your way, and from now on do not sin again.” Mercy does not call sin nothing; it calls the sinner by name, lifts her up, and sends her into a new life. This is what happens in every confession of the Great Fast. We come holding the stones we wanted to throw at others, and we go away holding nothing but his word: go, and do not sin again.
outline: Opening
Ask: am I holding a stone for someone today?
Point 1 · Waterless clouds
A life that promises and does not give.
Point 2 · The Lord rebuke you
Leaving judgment to God.
Point 3 · Misery and mercy
Jesus, the woman, and the stones laid down.
Take-home line
“Neither do I condemn you. Go your way, and from now on do not sin again.”
live: Put down the stone (John 8:7)
Name one person you have condemned in your heart or in your words, and pray for them by name today.
Go to confession (John 8:11)
Make your Lenten confession this week if you have not yet done so, and hear the words: go, and do not sin again.
2027-03-10.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you bent down and wrote on the ground, and the stones fell from the hands of the accusers. Take from us every stone we hold against others, and save us from becoming waterless clouds and fruitless trees. Look on our misery with your mercy, call us by name, and send us out to begin again, never to return to our sin. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana we stand where the woman stood, before the One who alone is without sin, and he does not condemn us but gives us himself as the food of a new life.

2027-03-11.title: Fifth Thursday of the Great Fast
2027-03-11.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
2027-03-11.alt: Season of the Great Fast (Sauma Ramba).
2027-03-11.verse: for, while physical training is of some value, godliness is valuable in every way, holding promise for both the present life and the life to come.
theo: Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker in Ephesus, as a coach writes to an athlete. The Greek world loved its gymnasium, and Paul borrows its language: “Train yourself in godliness, for, while physical training is of some value, godliness is valuable in every way, holding promise for both the present life and the life to come.” He does not despise the body's training; he simply sets it in its place. The body's fitness serves this life; godliness, eusebeia, a life turned reverently toward God, serves this life and the next. Like any training, it needs daily practice, a coach, and the willingness to be tired. Before dawn in many Kerala villages the young men of the kalari stretch and leap and repeat the same movements until they become second nature; no one becomes a master of kalaripayattu by reading about it. The Great Fast is the Church's season of training: the same prayers each morning and evening, the same small refusals at the table, the same Way of the Cross each Friday, until the soul learns new reflexes. Paul also warns Timothy to “Have nothing to do with profane myths and old wives' tales”, idle stories that fill the mind and starve the soul; today they come to us through the endless scrolling of our phones. And he gives the reason for all the effort: “For to this end we toil and struggle, because we have our hope set on the living God, who is the Savior of all people, especially of those who believe.” We do not train to impress anyone. We train because we hope.

In the Gospel Jesus takes the Twelve aside and tells them, for the third time in Luke, what is waiting at the end of the road: “See, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything that is written about the Son of Man by the prophets will be accomplished. For he will be handed over to the Gentiles; and he will be mocked and insulted and spat upon. After they have flogged him, they will kill him, and on the third day he will rise again.” Every word is clear. And yet Luke tells us three times over that they did not grasp it: “But they understood nothing about all these things; in fact, what he said was hidden from them, and they did not grasp what was said.” They had walked with him for years, seen his miracles, heard his parables, and still the Cross made no sense to them. The very next scene in Luke is a blind beggar at Jericho who cries out, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!”, and receives his sight (Luke 18:38). Those who walked beside Jesus could not see; the blind man by the road could. Only after Easter would the risen Lord open their minds to understand the Scriptures. In ten days we enter the Great Week. We too may know every word of the Passion story and still not understand it. Let us ask, like the beggar of Jericho, for eyes to see that the road up to Jerusalem is the road to glory.
outline: Opening
Ask: what am I training myself for this Lent?
Point 1 · Train yourself in godliness
The soul's gymnasium.
Point 2 · Going up to Jerusalem
The third foretelling of the Passion.
Point 3 · Hidden from them
Asking for eyes to see the Cross.
Take-home line
“Godliness is valuable in every way.”
live: One daily exercise (1 Timothy 4:7)
Choose one spiritual exercise, the same each day until Easter: a psalm, a decade of the Rosary, ten minutes of the Gospel, and do not miss a day.
Fast from idle stories (1 Timothy 4:7)
Keep your phone away for one hour each evening this week, and give that hour to prayer or to your family.
2027-03-11.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you set your face to go up to Jerusalem, knowing that you would be mocked, insulted, flogged and killed, and that on the third day you would rise. Train us in godliness through the discipline of this Great Fast, and set our hope on the living God. Open the eyes of our hearts, as you opened the eyes of the blind man at Jericho, so that we may understand your Cross and follow you to your glory. Amen.
altar: The Holy Qurbana is the school in which Christ trains us in godliness: day after day the same words and gestures form our hearts, until we understand the mystery of his Passion and Resurrection that we celebrate.

2027-03-12.title: Fifth Friday of the Great Fast
2027-03-12.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Caleb asks for the hill country
Put on the armour of light
2027-03-12.alt: Season of the Great Fast (Sauma Ramba). A Friday of abstinence from meat; the Way of the Cross is prayed in parishes and homes.
2027-03-12.verse: Very truly, I tell you, before Abraham was, I am.
theo: “The LORD appeared to Abraham by the oaks of Mamre, as he sat at the entrance of his tent in the heat of the day.” Three travellers appear in the shimmering noon, and the old man, who could have stayed in the shade, runs to meet them and bows to the ground: “My lord, if I find favor with you, do not pass by your servant.” He offers “a little water” and “a little bread”, and then sets out a feast: cakes of the finest flour, a tender calf, curds and milk, and “he stood by them under the tree while they ate.” Abraham does not know at first whom he is serving; the Letter to the Hebrews remembers that “by doing that some have entertained angels without knowing it” (Hebrews 13:2). The guests bring a promise: Sarah, long past the age of childbearing, will have a son. Listening behind the tent flap, Sarah laughs to herself. The LORD answers with the question that runs through the whole Bible: “Is anything too wonderful for the LORD?” Many Fathers saw in the three visitors, addressed as one Lord, a first hint of the mystery of the Holy Trinity, and the Eastern Churches have painted this scene as the icon of the Trinity's hospitality. The second reading shows us another old man who did not settle into the shade. Caleb, one of the two spies who had trusted God forty-five years earlier, comes to Joshua at the age of eighty-five: “I am still as strong today as I was on the day that Moses sent me.” He does not ask for a quiet field but for the hill country where the strongest enemies lived, because “I wholeheartedly followed the LORD my God.” Age is no retirement from faith. Among us there are grandparents who still walk to the first Qurbana before dawn on every day of the Great Fast, and who carry the whole family in their prayer. They are our Calebs.

Paul gives the Romans one debt that can never be paid off: “Owe no one anything, except to love one another; for the one who loves another has fulfilled the law.” Then he sounds a morning bell: “the night is far gone, the day is near. Let us then lay aside the works of darkness and put on the armor of light.” In the summer of 386, in a garden in Milan, a brilliant young teacher of rhetoric named Augustine, weeping over the slavery of his own desires, heard a child's voice chanting “take up and read”. He opened the letters of Paul and his eyes fell on these very words: “let us live honorably as in the day, not in reveling and drunkenness, not in debauchery and licentiousness, not in quarreling and jealousy. Instead, put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires.” He wrote later in his Confessions that at that moment the light of certainty flooded his heart. In the Gospel Jesus speaks in the temple with hearers who are scandalised by his claims: “Very truly, I tell you, whoever keeps my word will never see death.” They answer that Abraham died, and the prophets too. Jesus replies: “Your ancestor Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day; he saw it and was glad.” And then the words that sum up John's Gospel: “Very truly, I tell you, before Abraham was, I am.” I AM is the name God gave to Moses at the burning bush (Exodus 3:14). Some of his hearers took up stones, and Jesus went out of the temple. When John writes of “the Jews” in such debates he is speaking of particular opponents of Jesus in that hour, not of the Jewish people, to whom Jesus, Mary and the apostles belonged; the Church firmly rejects any blame of the Jewish people for the rejection or the death of Christ. The question is put to every one of us: who do I say that he is? The One who sat at Abraham's table is the One who now calls us to his, and before whom every Friday of the fast we kneel at the foot of the Cross.
outline: Opening
Ask: do I let the Lord pass by, or do I run to meet him?
Point 1 · By the oaks of Mamre
Hospitality and the God for whom nothing is too wonderful.
Point 2 · Caleb at eighty-five
A heart that follows the Lord wholeheartedly.
Point 3 · Put on the Lord Jesus Christ
The debt of love and the armour of light.
Point 4 · Before Abraham was, I am
Who Jesus is.
Take-home line
“Very truly, I tell you, before Abraham was, I am.”
live: Welcome a guest (Genesis 18:2)
This week, invite to your table someone who seldom receives an invitation: a widow, a student far from home, a lonely neighbour.
Pray the Way of the Cross (John 8:58)
Keep the Way of the Cross today, and at each station say once: Jesus, you are the I AM, have mercy on me.
2027-03-12.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you are the I AM, who was before Abraham and who sat at his table by the oaks of Mamre. Do not pass by your servants. Teach us to welcome you in every guest, to follow you wholeheartedly like Caleb even in old age, and to pay every day the debt of love. Clothe us with yourself, the armour of light, and on this Friday of the fast keep us close to your Cross, so that we may rejoice to see your day. Amen.
altar: Abraham stood by his guests while they ate; at the Holy Qurbana the Lord himself prepares the table and feeds us, and the One who is before Abraham becomes our food.

2027-03-13.title: Fifth Saturday of the Great Fast
2027-03-13.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Love is the greatest of all
2027-03-13.alt: Season of the Great Fast (Sauma Ramba).
2027-03-13.verse: Therefore what God has joined together, let no one separate.
theo: We usually hear the thirteenth chapter of First Corinthians at weddings, and it belongs there. But Paul did not write it for a bride and groom. He wrote it for a quarrelsome parish in a rich port city, where believers competed over spiritual gifts, divided into parties, and went to court against one another. So he begins by emptying every gift of its value if love is missing: “If I speak in the tongues of mortals and of angels, but do not have love, I am a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal. And if I have prophetic powers, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing.” Even heroic giving counts for nothing without it. Then he describes love not with feelings but with verbs, things love does and does not do: “Love is patient; love is kind; love is not envious or boastful or arrogant or rude. It does not insist on its own way; it is not irritable or resentful; it does not rejoice in wrongdoing, but rejoices in the truth. It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.” An old retreat preacher used to tell his listeners to read these lines again, putting their own name in place of the word love, and to stop at the first line where it became untrue. Only one Name fits every line: Jesus. Corinth was famous for its bronze mirrors, which gave back a blurred and darkened image; Paul uses them for our present knowledge of God: “For now we see in a mirror, dimly, but then we will see face to face.” Prophecies, tongues and knowledge will pass; “And now faith, hope, and love abide, these three; and the greatest of these is love.”

In the Gospel some Pharisees test Jesus with a question much debated among the teachers of his day: “Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife?” Jesus asks what Moses commanded, and they answer that Moses allowed a certificate of dismissal. Jesus goes back further than Moses, to the beginning: “Because of your hardness of heart he wrote this commandment for you. But from the beginning of creation, ‘God made them male and female.’ ‘For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.’ So they are no longer two, but one flesh. Therefore what God has joined together, let no one separate.” The Church has kept this word faithfully: a valid sacramental marriage, once consummated, cannot be dissolved by any human power. This is not a heavy burden laid on weak shoulders; it is a gift of grace, for Christ who asks it gives the strength to live it. At a Syro-Malabar wedding the bridegroom ties the minnu around the bride's neck and places the manthrakodi upon her, both blessed by the priest, signs of a bond meant to last until death. Paul's hymn is the daily bread of such a marriage: patient, kind, not irritable, bearing and enduring all things. At the same time the Church does not forget those whose marriages have been wounded or broken. They remain her children, are welcome in the parish, are accompanied with care, and may seek the help of the Church's tribunals to examine whether a true marriage existed. The Great Fast is a good time for every married couple to renew their promise, and for every family to pray for the marriages that are struggling.
outline: Opening
Ask: if I put my name in place of love, where does the sentence become untrue?
Point 1 · Without love, nothing
Gifts, knowledge and sacrifice emptied of value.
Point 2 · Love is patient, love is kind
The verbs of love in daily life.
Point 3 · What God has joined
Marriage from the beginning, and grace to live it.
Take-home line
“Therefore what God has joined together, let no one separate.”
live: Read 1 Corinthians 13 with your name (1 Corinthians 13:4)
Read verses 4 to 7 slowly, putting your own name in place of love, and choose the one line you will practise today.
Renew your promise (Mark 10:9)
If you are married, pray tonight with your spouse for your marriage; if not, pray for a couple you know who are struggling.
2027-03-13.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you are the love that is patient and kind, that bears all things and never ends. Without you we are noisy gongs and clanging cymbals. Make us patient and kind in our homes; strengthen husbands and wives to remain one flesh, as God joined them from the beginning; heal the wounds of broken marriages and console those who suffer from them; and bring us all at last from the dim mirror to see you face to face. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana Christ, the Bridegroom, gives himself to the Church his bride; every Christian marriage draws from this altar the love that never ends.

2027-03-15.title: Sixth Monday of the Great Fast
2027-03-15.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: I have come as light into the world
2027-03-15.alt: Season of the Great Fast (Sauma Ramba). The last full week of the fast before Hosanna Sunday.
2027-03-15.verse: I have come as light into the world, so that everyone who believes in me should not remain in the darkness.
theo: The sixth week of the Great Fast opens with one of the warmest pages Paul ever wrote. He had been forced to leave Thessalonica after only a few weeks, and he worried that the young Church would not survive persecution. So he sent Timothy back, and Timothy has now returned with good news. Paul can hardly contain himself: “For we now live, if you continue to stand firm in the Lord. How can we thank God enough for you in return for all the joy that we feel before our God because of you?” The apostle's own life seems to depend on the faith of his people. Then he prays for them: “And may the Lord make you increase and abound in love for one another and for all, just as we abound in love for you. And may he so strengthen your hearts in holiness that you may be blameless before our God and Father at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his saints.” This is what every good pastor, catechist and parent feels. We do not live for ourselves; we live when those entrusted to us stand firm. In these last weeks of the fast many families are far apart: children studying in Bengaluru or Delhi, parents working in the Gulf, grandparents keeping the house at home. Paul's prayer can become our prayer for them: that the Lord will make love increase, and strengthen hearts in holiness, until we meet face to face.

The Gospel is the last public word of Jesus in the first half of John's Gospel. After this he will speak only to his disciples at the supper. “Then Jesus cried aloud”: he raises his voice, as if to be heard by everyone who will ever live. “Whoever believes in me believes not in me but in him who sent me. And whoever sees me sees him who sent me.” To look at Jesus is to see the Father. Then comes the reason he came: “I have come as light into the world, so that everyone who believes in me should not remain in the darkness.” He does not come to condemn: “for I came not to judge the world, but to save the world.” And yet a word refused does not disappear; “on the last day the word that I have spoken will serve as judge.” The same light that saves also shows what we have chosen. The fast has been a slow walk out of the dark rooms of the heart into this light. In the Holy Qurbana the light is not only spoken but given, for the Word who speaks to us is the Bread who feeds us. As the week of the Passion draws near, Jesus still cries aloud to us: do not remain in the darkness.
outline: Opening
Ask: who lives because I stand firm?
Point 1 · Now we live
Paul's joy at the faith of his people.
Point 2 · Light into the world
To see Jesus is to see the Father.
Point 3 · The word that judges
Not condemned, but answerable.
Take-home line
“I have come as light into the world.”
live: Pray for the far-away (1 Thessalonians 3:12)
Each evening this week name one family member who lives far from home, and pray Paul's prayer for them.
Step into the light
Before Hosanna Sunday, bring one dark corner of your life to the sacrament of reconciliation.
2027-03-15.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, light of the world, you came not to judge us but to save us. Do not let us remain in the darkness. Make us increase and abound in love for one another and for all, and strengthen our hearts in holiness, so that we may stand firm in you and be blameless before the Father when you come with all your saints. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the Word who cried aloud in the temple speaks to us again, and then gives himself as the Bread of life; whoever receives him receives the Father who sent him.

2027-03-16.title: Sixth Tuesday of the Great Fast
2027-03-16.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: The Lord knows how to rescue the godly
2027-03-16.alt: Season of the Great Fast (Sauma Ramba).
2027-03-16.verse: Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! How often have I desired to gather your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!
theo: The Second Letter of Peter was written to Christians troubled by teachers who mocked God's judgement and lived as they pleased. Peter answers with three examples from the Scriptures: the angels who sinned, the world of Noah's flood, and the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah. In each case God did not let evil have the last word. But in each case he also saved someone. He “saved Noah, a herald of righteousness, with seven others”, and “he rescued Lot, a righteous man greatly distressed by the licentiousness of the lawless (for that righteous man, living among them day after day, was tormented in his righteous soul by their lawless deeds that he saw and heard)”. Peter's conclusion is full of comfort: “the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trial.” Lot was no great hero; Genesis tells us that he lingered, and the angels had to take him by the hand. Yet he had not grown used to the evil around him; it tormented his soul. That is a sign of life. Many of us live, study or work among habits that slowly dull the conscience. The Great Fast asks: am I still distressed by what is wrong, or have I made my peace with it? The Lord who took Lot by the hand can lead us out too.

In the Gospel some Pharisees come to warn Jesus: “Get away from here, for Herod wants to kill you.” Not every Pharisee was his enemy; some here seem to want to protect him. Jesus will not run. “Go and tell that fox for me, ‘Listen, I am casting out demons and performing cures today and tomorrow, and on the third day I finish my work.’” Herod is a fox, cunning but small; Jesus' path is set by the Father, and it leads to Jerusalem and to the third day. Then his voice changes, and he speaks not in anger but in grief: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! How often have I desired to gather your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!” This is the voice of a mother, not a judge. The image is tender and costly: a hen spreads her wings over her chicks when danger comes, and takes the fire or the hawk on herself. That is what Jesus will do on the Cross. His lament is not a condemnation of the Jewish people, whom God has never ceased to love; it is the grief of love over every human heart that refuses to be gathered, and so it is addressed to us. Next Sunday we will cry “Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord”; today we ask whether we are willing to be gathered under his wings.
outline: Opening
Ask: am I still troubled by what is wrong around me?
Point 1 · The Lord knows how to rescue
Noah, Lot, and the godly in every age.
Point 2 · Tell that fox
Jesus does not turn from his road.
Point 3 · As a hen gathers her brood
The grief of love, and our answer.
Take-home line
“How often have I desired to gather your children together.”
live: Keep your conscience awake (2 Peter 2:8)
Name one habit around you that no longer troubles you, and ask the Lord to make you sensitive again.
Come under his wings (Luke 13:34)
Spend ten quiet minutes before the Blessed Sacrament this week, simply letting yourself be gathered.
2027-03-16.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you set your face toward Jerusalem and did not turn back. As a hen gathers her brood under her wings, you long to gather us. Keep our consciences awake among the evils of our time, take us by the hand when we linger, and make us willing to be gathered under your wings. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the Lord who longed to gather Jerusalem's children gathers us around one altar, and gives us the Body that was given up for us, as a mother bird shields her young with her own body.

2027-03-17.title: Sixth Wednesday of the Great Fast
2027-03-17.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Whoever loves a brother or sister lives in the light
Where two or three are gathered
2027-03-17.alt: Season of the Great Fast (Sauma Ramba). In the Latin calendar today is the memorial of St Patrick.
2027-03-17.verse: For where two or three are gathered in my name, I am there among them.
theo: John writes as an old man to children in the faith, and he says something that sounds like a riddle: “Beloved, I am writing you no new commandment, but an old commandment that you have had from the beginning.” And then, almost at once: “Yet I am writing you a new commandment.” The commandment of love is old, because it was given at the beginning and is written in every human heart. It is new, because in Christ it has been lived to the end, “because the darkness is passing away and the true light is already shining.” Then John draws a line no one can argue with: “Whoever says, ‘I am in the light,’ while hating a brother or sister, is still in the darkness. Whoever loves a brother or sister lives in the light, and in such a person there is no cause for stumbling.” Hatred blinds: “whoever hates another believer is in the darkness, walks in the darkness, and does not know the way to go, because the darkness has brought on blindness.” Many Kerala families carry old quarrels, over a boundary wall, a share of family property, a wedding where someone was not honoured. They can last for generations, and people still come to the same church on Sunday and sit apart. John's word is plain: no amount of fasting puts us in the light while such a quarrel is kept alive by our own choice.

The Gospel gives the way out, step by step. “If another member of the church sins against you, go and point out the fault when the two of you are alone.” Not gossip first, not a public scene, but a quiet word face to face. “If the member listens to you, you have regained that one.” The goal is not to win an argument but to win back a brother or sister. Only if that fails do others become involved, and then the Church; and the Church receives the power to bind and to loose, which the Lord exercises above all in the sacrament of reconciliation. Then Jesus speaks of prayer: “if two of you agree on earth about anything you ask, it will be done for you by my Father in heaven. For where two or three are gathered in my name, I am there among them.” Notice the order: first reconciliation, then agreement in prayer, then his presence. Two people who were not speaking, and who come together again in his name, become a place where Christ stands. The Latin Church today remembers St Patrick, who returned as a missionary to the land where he had been a slave, and made of his former captors a people gathered in Christ's name.
outline: Opening
Ask: is there someone I have not spoken to in years?
Point 1 · An old commandment, a new commandment
Love, as old as creation and as new as the Cross.
Point 2 · Go and point out the fault
Winning back, not winning.
Point 3 · Two or three in my name
Reconciled, agreed, and Christ among us.
Take-home line
“Where two or three are gathered in my name, I am there among them.”
live: Take the first step (Matthew 18:15)
Before Pesaha, speak privately and gently to one person with whom you have an unresolved quarrel.
Pray with someone (Matthew 18:19)
Agree with one family member on a single intention, and pray for it together every night until Easter.
2027-03-17.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, true light already shining, drive the darkness of hatred from our hearts. Give us courage to go to those who have wronged us, not to win, but to win them back. Gather us in your name, so that we may agree in prayer and know that you are among us. Amen.
altar: Before the anaphora of the Holy Qurbana we exchange the sign of peace, because no one can bring a gift to the altar while refusing peace to a brother or sister; then Christ is truly present among those gathered in his name.

2027-03-18.title: Sixth Thursday of the Great Fast
2027-03-18.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
2027-03-18.alt: Season of the Great Fast (Sauma Ramba). In the Latin calendar today is the memorial of St Cyril of Jerusalem. Tomorrow is the Fortieth Friday, and the feast of St Joseph.
theo: Peter's language about the false teachers is some of the strongest in the New Testament. They are “like irrational animals, mere creatures of instinct”. “They have eyes full of adultery, insatiable for sin. They entice unsteady souls. They have hearts trained in greed.” He compares them to Balaam, the prophet who “loved the wages of doing wrong” and had to be corrected by his own donkey. And then comes an image every farmer in Kerala understands at the end of a dry summer: “These are waterless springs and mists driven by a storm.” A spring that promises water and gives none is worse than no spring at all; the traveller walks to it and finds dust. A mist promises rain and blows away. Peter is speaking of teachers, but the warning reaches every Christian. We can look like a spring: baptised, confirmed, present at the feasts, with a holy picture in the house. And yet, when a thirsty person comes to us, a lonely neighbour, a child with questions, a poor man at the gate, do they find water? “Hearts trained in greed” is a striking phrase: greed is learned by practice, and so is generosity. The fast is a training of the heart in the other direction.

In the Gospel John the Baptist speaks to the crowds who came out to be baptised. He refuses to let them rest on their ancestry: “Bear fruits worthy of repentance. Do not begin to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our ancestor’; for I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children to Abraham.” We could say, “We are St Thomas Christians; our families have been Christian for centuries.” It is a great gift, but it cannot replace fruit. “Even now the ax is lying at the root of the trees.” Then the crowd asks the most honest question in the Gospel: “What then should we do?” John's answer is not mystical; it is practical and almost embarrassing in its simplicity: “Whoever has two coats must share with anyone who has none; and whoever has food must do likewise.” Most of us have more than two shirts, and food in the kitchen tonight. The fruit of repentance can be counted in clothes given away and meals shared. The Latin Church today remembers St Cyril of Jerusalem, whose instructions to those about to be baptised at Easter still survive; like John, he taught that conversion must show itself in a changed life.
outline: Opening
Ask: when someone thirsty comes to me, do they find water?
Point 1 · Waterless springs
The danger of a faith that promises and does not give.
Point 2 · Do not say, ‘We have Abraham’
Heritage is a gift, not a substitute.
Point 3 · What then should we do?
Two coats and food to share.
Take-home line
“Bear fruits worthy of repentance.”
live: Empty one shelf (Luke 3:11)
Before Pesaha, give away clothes you do not wear to someone who needs them.
Share a meal
Invite someone who will be alone during the Week of the Passion to eat with your family.
2027-03-18.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, fountain of living water, do not let us be waterless springs. Train our hearts in generosity instead of greed. Free us from resting on our heritage, and make us bear fruits worthy of repentance, sharing our coats and our bread with those who have none. Amen.
altar: In the Holy Qurbana Christ is the spring that never runs dry: he gives himself whole to everyone who comes, and sends us out to give as we have received.

2027-03-19.title: Fortieth Friday of the Great Fast · St Joseph, Spouse of the Blessed Virgin Mary
2027-03-19.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
2027-03-19.alt: Season of the Great Fast (Sauma Ramba). Fortieth Friday (Nalpatham Velli), the sixth Friday of the fast; longer forms in the calendar: Romans 15:1–13; John 11:1–45. St Joseph, Spouse of the Blessed Virgin Mary: Isaiah 41:8–16; Acts 19:11–20; 2 Corinthians 10:3–11; Matthew 1:18–25. In 2027 the two fall on the same day; follow your eparchy's directions on which readings are used and on the penance of the day.
2027-03-19.verse: Did I not tell you that if you believed, you would see the glory of God?
theo: Today is the fortieth day since the Great Fast began on Monday 8 February. The Lord fasted forty days in the desert; Moses stayed forty days on the mountain; Elijah walked forty days to Horeb; and the Church, counting with them, keeps this Friday as the Fortieth Friday, Nalpatham Velli. Our forefathers in Kerala called the whole season the fifty-day fast, because it runs on through the Week of the Passion to Easter; the forty days are complete today, and what remains is the road with Christ to Jerusalem. In many parishes the Way of the Cross is made with special devotion today, and some climb a hill shrine on foot, carrying a small cross. In 2027 this day is also the feast of St Joseph, the just man who guarded the Lord's childhood. It is a fitting meeting: the man of silence who obeyed in the night stands at the door of the week in which his foster Son will obey the Father unto death.

The first reading is short and quiet. After the destruction of Sodom, “Abraham went early in the morning to the place where he had stood before the Lord; and he looked down toward Sodom and Gomorrah and toward all the land of the Plain and saw the smoke of the land going up like the smoke of a furnace.” The day before, at that very place, he had bargained with God for the city: fifty righteous, forty-five, forty, thirty, twenty, ten. Not even ten were found.
