Yet his prayer was not lost: “So it was that, when God destroyed the cities of the Plain, God remembered Abraham, and sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow.” No intercession is wasted. The second reading tells of a near civil war. The tribes who had settled east of the Jordan built a great altar by the river, and the other tribes, fearing rebellion and a second altar against the Lord's, gathered at Shiloh to make war. They sent Phinehas and ten chiefs to ask: “What is this treachery that you have committed against the God of Israel?” The rest of the chapter tells that the altar was meant only as a witness that both sides of the river belonged to the one Lord, and war was avoided because they spoke before they fought. Paul gives the Christian rule for every such tension: “Welcome one another, therefore, just as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God.” He ends with a blessing worth praying every day of Holy Week: “May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that you may abound in hope by the power of the Holy Spirit.”

The Gospel brings us to Bethany, to the tomb of Lazarus, the last and greatest sign in John's Gospel before the Passion. “Then Jesus, again greatly disturbed, came to the tomb. It was a cave, and a stone was lying against it. Jesus said, ‘Take away the stone.’” Martha, practical as always, protests: “Lord, already there is a stench because he has been dead four days.” Jesus answers with the word that is today's key: “Did I not tell you that if you believed, you would see the glory of God?” The stone is rolled away. Jesus lifts his eyes and thanks the Father aloud, “so that they may believe that you sent me.” Then “he cried with a loud voice, ‘Lazarus, come out!’ The dead man came out, his hands and feet bound with strips of cloth, and his face wrapped in a cloth. Jesus said to them, ‘Unbind him, and let him go.’” Lazarus returns to ordinary life and will die again; it is a sign, not yet the Resurrection. But it points to the Easter that is coming, when the stone will be rolled away from another tomb, and the grave cloths will be left lying, because the One who comes out will never die again. Notice too that Jesus gives others a part: they must take away the stone, and they must unbind him. The Church does this still. Christ alone gives life; through the ministry of his Church the bonds of sin are loosed in the sacrament of reconciliation. On this Fortieth Friday, what stone needs to be rolled away, and what bands still hold us?

The readings of St Joseph speak of a man who did not fear. “Do not fear, for I am with you, do not be afraid, for I am your God; I will strengthen you, I will help you, I will uphold you with my victorious right hand,” says the Lord through Isaiah. Joseph needed that word. He found the woman he was to marry with child, and “being a righteous man and unwilling to expose her to public disgrace, planned to dismiss her quietly.” Then the angel came in a dream: “Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to take Mary as your wife, for the child conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit. She will bear a son, and you are to name him Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins.” And the Gospel says simply: “When Joseph awoke from sleep, he did as the angel of the Lord commanded him.” Not one word of Joseph is recorded in the Gospels. He speaks through obedience, work and care. He names the child Jesus, “the Lord saves”, and so gives the Son of God his place in the house of David. Pope Francis called him a father in the shadows, and Pope Pius IX declared him Patron of the Universal Church. In many Kerala homes and parishes his feast is marked by a meal for the poor, the oottu, where an elderly man, a woman and a child are honoured at table in memory of the Holy Family of Nazareth. As we enter the Week of the Passion, Joseph teaches us to do what the Lord asks, without speeches, and to trust that “God is with us”, even in the night.
conn: Abraham's intercession.
Abraham pleads for Sodom down to ten righteous (Genesis 18:23–32); God remembers him and saves Lot (Genesis 19:29). “The prayer of the righteous is powerful and effective” (James 5:16).
The altar as a witness.

The eastern tribes explain that their altar is not for sacrifice but a witness between them and the other tribes that the Lord is God (Joshua 22:26–29, 34). Speaking first saved Israel from war; Christ is our one altar and our peace (Ephesians 2:14).
The root of Jesse.
Paul quotes Isaiah: “The root of Jesse shall come” (Romans 15:12; Isaiah 11:10). Joseph, son of David, son of Jesse, gives Jesus his legal place in that royal line (Matthew 1:16, 20).
I will open your graves.

Ezekiel's vision of the dry bones (Ezekiel 37:12–13) is fulfilled first in sign at Bethany and then fully in the Resurrection of Christ and of all who belong to him (John 5:28–29; 1 Corinthians 15:20–23).
The grave cloths.
Lazarus comes out still bound (John 11:44); at Easter the linen wrappings are left lying in the empty tomb (John 20:6–7), for Christ rises never to die again (Romans 6:9).
The two Josephs.
Joseph the patriarch, the dreamer, saved his family in Egypt (Genesis 50:20); Joseph of Nazareth, guided by dreams, saved the Saviour by taking him to Egypt and back (Matthew 2:13–15, 19–23).
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the Lord who called Lazarus from the tomb gives us his own risen Body, the pledge that he will raise us up on the last day.
Joseph held the Son of God in his arms and fed him with the work of his hands; at every Holy Qurbana the Church receives the same Lord, given to us as the Bread of life.
outline: Opening
Forty days complete: what has the fast done in me?
Point 1 · God remembered Abraham
No intercession is wasted.
Point 2 · Welcome one another
Speak before you fight; one altar, one Lord.
Point 3 · Lazarus, come out
The stone, the voice, the unbinding.
Point 4 · Joseph did as the angel commanded
Silent obedience, fearless trust.
Closing image
A stone rolled back from a tomb at Bethany, and a carpenter rising in the night to do what God asked.
Take-home line
“Did I not tell you that if you believed, you would see the glory of God?”
live: Make the Way of the Cross (Nalpatham Velli)
Walk the stations today, in church or on a hill shrine, offering the forty days of your fast.
Intercede by name (Genesis 19:29)
Write the names of three people who are far from God and pray for them every day of the Week of the Passion.
Let yourself be unbound (John 11:44)
Make your Easter confession before Pesaha, and let the Lord loose what binds you.
Keep St Joseph's table
Share a meal with the poor today, or give for one, in honour of the Holy Family.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

Lazarus four days in the tomb is the soul buried under the habit of sin. When Christ calls, the sinner comes out by confessing; but he comes out still bound, and the Lord says to his ministers, Unbind him: what the Church looses on earth is loosed in heaven.
St Bernard of Clairvaux (in substance)

Joseph is the faithful and prudent servant whom the Lord set over his household: the comfort of his Mother, the provider for his own humanity, and the one trusted helper in the great work of our salvation. What God gave to the patriarch Joseph, to store bread for a people, he gave to this Joseph, to guard the living Bread from heaven.
magis: Catechism 994
Jesus links faith in the resurrection to his own person: “I am the resurrection and the life.” He gives a sign of it by raising the dead, and so announces his own Resurrection.
Catechism 646
The raising of Lazarus was a return to ordinary earthly life; Christ's Resurrection is essentially different, for his risen body passes into a life beyond time and space.
Catechism 2635
Intercession is a prayer of petition that leads us to pray as Jesus did; since Abraham, it belongs to a heart attuned to God's mercy.
Catechism 1655
Christ chose to be born and grow up in the bosom of the holy family of Joseph and Mary; the Church is nothing other than the family of God.
Pope Francis, Patris Corde (2020)
Joseph is a beloved, tender and obedient father, accepting and creatively courageous, a working father who lived in the shadows; in him Jesus saw the tender love of God.
saints: Today

Fortieth Friday of the Great Fast: the Way of the Cross and, in many places, pilgrimages on foot to hill shrines. Feast of St Joseph, Spouse of the Blessed Virgin Mary, Patron of the Universal Church; in many places a meal for the poor (oottu) in honour of the Holy Family.
2027-03-19.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, resurrection and life, you wept at the tomb of your friend and called him out with a loud voice. On this fortieth day of our fast, roll away the stones that shut us in, call us out of every grave of sin, and let your Church unbind us and set us free. Through the prayers of St Joseph, the just man who did all that the angel commanded, give us his silent obedience and his fearless trust, and bring us with him to the glory of God. To you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be glory for ever. Amen.

2027-03-20.title: Sixth Saturday of the Great Fast
2027-03-20.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
2027-03-20.alt: Season of the Great Fast (Sauma Ramba). Tomorrow is Hosanna Sunday, and the Week of the Passion begins.
2027-03-20.verse: The house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume.
theo: On the eve of Hosanna Sunday the Church sets two farewells side by side. Paul is on his way to Jerusalem and calls the elders of Ephesus to Miletus. He knows what is coming: “And now, as a captive to the Spirit, I am on my way to Jerusalem, not knowing what will happen to me there, except that the Holy Spirit testifies to me in every city that imprisonment and persecutions are waiting for me.” He is not afraid: “But I do not count my life of any value to myself, if only I may finish my course and the ministry that I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify to the good news of God's grace.” He charges the elders to shepherd “the church of God that he obtained with the blood of his own Son”, and gives them a saying of Jesus found nowhere else in Scripture: “It is more blessed to give than to receive.” Then “he knelt down with them all and prayed. There was much weeping among them all; they embraced Paul and kissed him.” Paul walks toward Jerusalem as his Master did, with his face set and his heart full of love for those he leaves behind. Every priest who has left a parish, every parent who has watched a child leave for a distant country, knows something of that shore at Miletus.

The Gospel takes us to Bethany “six days before the Passover”. Lazarus, raised from the dead, sits at the table; Martha serves, as she always does; and Mary does something no one expected. She “took a pound of costly perfume made of pure nard, anointed Jesus' feet, and wiped them with her hair. The house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume.” A pound of pure nard was worth a year's wages. Judas objects that it should have been sold for the poor, but John tells us his heart was not with the poor. Jesus defends her: “Leave her alone. She bought it so that she might keep it for the day of my burial.” Mary has understood what the disciples have not: that he is going to die, and that love does not calculate at such a moment. Her gift is extravagant, and the whole house is filled with it. Tomorrow we will wave palms and cry Hosanna; this evening the Gospel asks what we will pour out at his feet in the coming week. In many homes the days before Pesaha are spent cleaning the house and preparing for the Pesaha appam. Let the house be filled too with the fragrance of prayer, forgiveness and generous love.
outline: Opening
Ask: what will I pour out at his feet this week?
Point 1 · A captive to the Spirit
Paul walks toward Jerusalem.
Point 2 · More blessed to give
The shepherd's last charge.
Point 3 · The fragrance filled the house
Mary's extravagant love.
Take-home line
“The house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume.”
live: Prepare the house (John 12:3)
With your family, make the house ready for the Week of the Passion: a cleaned prayer corner, a cross in its place, the television quieter.
Give extravagantly (Acts 20:35)
Give one gift this week that costs you something, without calculating.
2027-03-20.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, six days before the Passover you sat at table in Bethany, and Mary poured out her costly perfume at your feet. Give us her love that does not calculate, and Paul's courage to finish the course. As we enter the Week of your Passion, fill our homes with the fragrance of prayer and generous love. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the Lord whose body Mary anointed for burial gives that same body to us, risen and glorious; the Church obtained by his blood is gathered at his table.

2027-03-22.title: Seventh Monday of the Great Fast · Monday of Hasha Week
2027-03-22.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: The Son is superior to the angels
2027-03-22.alt: Hasha Week (Holy Week), the last week of the Great Fast. From today until the end of the season of the Dedication of the Church, the Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Order of the first Qudasha (of Mar Addai and Mari), as the calendar notes.
2027-03-22.verse: and not for the nation only, but to gather into one the dispersed children of God.
theo: The Hosanna is over, and the week the St Thomas Christians call Hasha has begun. Hasha is the Syriac word for suffering: this is the week of the Lord's Passion, the last and holiest week of the Great Fast. From today, the calendar notes, the Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Order of the first Qudasha, the anaphora of Mar Addai and Mari, until the end of the season of the Dedication of the Church. Kerala homes keep the week with a rhythm of their own. The tender palm leaves (kuruthola) blessed yesterday are put away carefully, because on Thursday a small cross made from them will crown the Pesaha appam. Houses are cleaned, the last Lenten confessions are made, and in many parishes the forty hours' adoration brings families to the church by turns, day and night, while pilgrims keep climbing Malayattoor. The Church opens this week with a story from the first family of Israel: the beloved son sent by his father to his brothers. “Now Israel loved Joseph more than any other of his children” (Genesis 37:3). Joseph dreams that his brothers' sheaves bow to his sheaf, and then that “the sun, the moon, and eleven stars were bowing down to me.” His brothers ask, “Are you indeed to reign over us?” “So his brothers were jealous of him, but his father kept the matter in mind.” Then Jacob sends him: “Come, I will send you to them.” He answered, “Here I am.” Joseph wanders in the fields until a stranger asks him, “What are you seeking?” and he answers, “I am seeking my brothers.” They see him from far off and say, “Here comes this dreamer. Come now, let us kill him and throw him into one of the pits”. Only Reuben pleads, “Let us not take his life.” From the earliest centuries the Fathers saw in Joseph a picture of Christ: the beloved Son, sent by the Father, who comes looking for his brothers, and whom they plot to destroy. The whole of Hasha week answers the stranger's question in the field. What is he seeking? He is seeking his brothers and sisters. He is seeking us.

The second reading tells of a quarrel that almost became a civil war. The tribes of Reuben and Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh, settled east of the Jordan, build a great altar by the river. The other tribes take it for rebellion, a rival altar, and gather to fight. The eastern tribes answer with a cry: “The LORD, God of gods! The LORD, God of gods! He knows; and let Israel itself know!” They did not build it for sacrifice, they explain, but so that in time to come no one could tell their children, “You have no portion in the LORD.” It was to be “a witness between us and you”, and they swear: “Far be it from us that we should rebel against the LORD”. A misunderstanding between brothers is healed because both sides stopped to listen before they struck. Holy Week asks the same of us: one altar, one Lord, one people. No family quarrel and no parish faction should still be standing on Pesaha evening, when the whole parish gathers at one altar for one Qurbana. The Epistle lifts our eyes to the One who will walk the way of the Cross this week. The letter to the Hebrews gathers the psalms to show that the Son is above every angel: “For to which of the angels did God ever say, ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’?” When he comes into the world, “Let all God's angels worship him.” To the Son God says: “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever”. Heaven and earth “will perish, but you remain”, and “your years will never end.” The prisoner who will be bound on Thursday night, mocked on Friday and laid in a tomb is the eternal Son. That is why the Passion is not only a sad story: it is God himself who suffers in the flesh for us.

The Gospel takes us into the council that met after the raising of Lazarus. The chief priests and the Pharisees are afraid: “If we let him go on like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and destroy both our holy place and our nation.” They lived under a foreign power that could crush a city for a single riot. Caiaphas, high priest that year, speaks with the cold arithmetic of power: “it is better for you to have one man die for the people than to have the whole nation destroyed.” John sees in these words a prophecy deeper than Caiaphas knew: Jesus was about to die for the nation, “and not for the nation only, but to gather into one the dispersed children of God.” We must read this carefully, as the Church does. The decision was taken by a few leaders in a frightened hour. The Church teaches that the Passion cannot be charged against all the Jews then living, nor against the Jews of today (Nostra Aetate 4; Catechism 597), and that all sinners were the authors of Christ's sufferings (Catechism 598). The question of this week is not who killed Jesus long ago, but whose sins he carried; and the answer is ours. Jesus withdraws to a town called Ephraim near the wilderness. In Jerusalem the pilgrims who have come early to purify themselves for the Passover ask one another in the temple, “What do you think? Surely he will not come to the festival, will he?” He will come. He will come on purpose, to be the one man who dies for the people, so that the scattered children of God, from Jerusalem to Kerala and to every land where our people now live, may be gathered into one.
conn: Hasha.
The Syriac word for suffering. The St Thomas Christians call Holy Week the Hasha week, the week of the Lord's Passion.
Joseph and Christ.
The beloved son sent by his father, hated by his brothers, sold, and raised up to save them: Stephen tells this story to the council (Acts 7:9–10), and the Fathers read it as a figure of Christ.
Here I am.
Joseph's answer echoes Abraham (Genesis 22:1) and Isaiah (Isaiah 6:8), and the Son's own word on entering the world: I have come to do your will (Hebrews 10:7).
The altar called Witness.
The eastern tribes named their altar Witness, “a witness between us that the LORD is God” (Joshua 22:34).
Hebrews and the psalms.
Hebrews 1:5–13 weaves Psalm 2:7, 2 Samuel 7:14, Psalm 45:6–7, Psalm 102:25–27 and Psalm 110:1 into one portrait of the Son.
An unwitting prophecy.
Caiaphas speaks of one man dying for the people; Jesus had said that he lays down his life for the sheep and has other sheep to gather into one flock (John 10:15–16).
outline: Opening
Ask: what am I seeking this week, and do I know that the Son is seeking me?
Point 1 · Here comes this dreamer
The beloved son sent to his brothers.
Point 2 · An altar of witness
Listening before we strike.
Point 3 · Above the angels
The eternal Son goes to the Cross.
Point 4 · One man for the people
To gather the dispersed children of God.
Take-home line
“to gather into one the dispersed children of God.”
live: Say Here I am (Genesis 37:13)
Begin each morning of Hasha week with Joseph's words, and do the first duty of the day willingly.
Heal one quarrel (Joshua 22:26–27)
Before Pesaha, go and listen to someone you have misunderstood or who has misunderstood you, and be reconciled.
Keep the kuruthola
Keep yesterday's blessed palm safely for the Pesaha appam, and pray before it as a family tonight.
Watch one hour
Take your turn at the forty hours' adoration, or make a visit to the Blessed Sacrament this week.
fathers: St Ambrose (in substance)

In holy Joseph we see Christ: sent by his father to his brothers, stripped of his robe, sold for silver, and afterwards the saviour of those who sold him. The brothers meant to put an end to his dreams, and by their very hatred the dream came true.
St Augustine (in substance)

Caiaphas spoke the truth without knowing it. A wicked man uttered a prophecy, not by his own holiness but because of the office he held, for Christ was indeed to die to gather the scattered children of God into one.
magis: Catechism 596
The religious authorities in Jerusalem were not unanimous about Jesus; the council's decision was taken in fear for the holy place and the nation.
Catechism 597
The responsibility for the trial of Jesus cannot be ascribed to the Jews in Jerusalem as a whole, nor extended to the Jews of other times and places (Nostra Aetate 4).
Catechism 598
Sinners themselves were the authors and ministers of all the sufferings that Christ endured.
Catechism 1169
Easter is the feast of feasts; Holy Week leads the Church to it.
2027-03-22.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, beloved Son of the Father, you came looking for your brothers and sisters, and you answered the Father, Here I am. In this Hasha week gather us, scattered by our sins and quarrels, into one family around your one altar. You are the eternal Son, whom the angels worship, and you chose to die for the people: let us not stand far off, but follow you to the Cross and to the joy of your Resurrection. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: The council said one man must die for the people. At every Holy Qurbana that one death is made present on the altar, and the scattered children of God are gathered into one body.
Joseph went looking for his brothers in the fields; in the Qurbana the Son comes looking for us, and we answer as Joseph did: Here I am.

2027-03-23.title: Seventh Tuesday of the Great Fast · Tuesday of Hasha Week
2027-03-23.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Joseph is sold by his brothers
Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth
2027-03-23.alt: Hasha Week (Holy Week), the last week of the Great Fast. Many parishes keep the forty hours' adoration and offer confessions through these days, so that all may come to the Pesaha Qurbana with a clean heart.
2027-03-23.verse: Very truly, I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains just a single grain; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.
theo: Yesterday the brothers saw Joseph coming; today they act. “So when Joseph came to his brothers, they stripped him of his robe, the long robe with sleeves that he wore; and they took him and threw him into a pit. The pit was empty; there was no water in it.” The next sentence is one of the coldest in the Bible: “Then they sat down to eat”. Their brother is in a dry well within earshot, and they eat. A caravan of traders appears, and Judah has an idea that sounds almost merciful: “What profit is it if we kill our brother and conceal his blood? Come, let us sell him to the Ishmaelites, and not lay our hands on him, for he is our brother, our own flesh.” And so Joseph is sold “for twenty pieces of silver”. Reuben comes back to the empty pit and cries, “The boy is gone; and I, where can I turn?” The brothers dip the robe in a goat's blood and let their father draw his own conclusion. Jacob tears his garments and “refused to be comforted”. The whole tragedy began with jealousy, the small, quiet sin that grows in families until a brother becomes a price. Many Kerala families know how a dispute over property or money can make strangers of those who shared one table. In Joseph the Fathers saw the Lord again: the beloved Son stripped of his garments (John 19:23), handed over for silver (Matthew 26:15), counted among the dead while he was still alive. Yet the pit is not the end of Joseph's story, and the tomb will not be the end of Christ's.

The second reading shows the opposite of Joseph's brothers: tribes who had every reason to suspect one another, and who chose to trust. When Phinehas the priest hears the explanation about the altar by the Jordan, he is satisfied, and he says: “Today we know that the LORD is among us, because you have not committed this treachery against the LORD”. The altar is named Witness, and “A long time afterward, when the LORD had given rest to Israel from all their enemies all around”, the land has peace. Where brothers keep faith with one another, the Lord is known to be among them. The Epistle shows us the high priest who will make that peace for ever. “Every high priest chosen from among mortals is put in charge of things pertaining to God on their behalf, to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins. He is able to deal gently with the ignorant and wayward, since he himself is subject to weakness”. Christ did not take this honour for himself; the Father called him: “You are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek.” Then comes a line that opens the door of Gethsemane two days early: “In the days of his flesh, Jesus offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to the one who was able to save him from death, and he was heard because of his reverent submission. Although he was a Son, he learned obedience through what he suffered”. He was heard: not by being spared the Cross, but by being raised from death. On Thursday we will thank God for the gift of the priesthood, born at the Last Supper; today we can pray for our priests, who are chosen from among us and share our weakness, so that they may deal gently with the wayward.

The Gospel brings strangers to the festival. “Now among those who went up to worship at the festival were some Greeks. They came to Philip, who was from Bethsaida in Galilee, and said to him, ‘Sir, we wish to see Jesus.’” In many churches those words are carved where only the preacher can read them, as a reminder of what the people really came for. Philip tells Andrew, and the two of them tell Jesus. His answer seems at first to ignore the request: “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.” Then he explains what that glory is: “Very truly, I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains just a single grain; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.” The Greeks will see him, but they will see him lifted up on the Cross, and the grain buried in the earth will rise as a harvest for every nation. Every farmer in Kerala knows that seed kept safe in the granary feeds no one. The St Thomas Christians have always believed that the apostle Thomas, too, was a grain that fell into the earth of India, and our Church is part of its fruit. Jesus adds the law of every disciple: “Those who love their life lose it, and those who hate their life in this world will keep it for eternal life. Whoever serves me must follow me, and where I am, there will my servant be also.” On Thursday that grain of wheat will be placed in our hands as the Bread of Life.
conn: Twenty and thirty pieces of silver.
Joseph is sold for twenty pieces of silver (Genesis 37:28); Judas agrees to hand Jesus over for thirty (Matthew 26:15).
The robe and the tunic.
Joseph's long robe is stripped from him and dipped in blood (Genesis 37:23, 31); the soldiers take Jesus' clothes and cast lots for his seamless tunic (John 19:23–24).
Sold, then saviour.
Later Joseph tells his brothers: God sent me before you to preserve life (Genesis 45:5). What was meant for evil, God turned to good (Genesis 50:20).
Melchizedek.
The priest-king of Salem who brought out bread and wine and blessed Abraham (Genesis 14:18–20); Psalm 110:4 calls the Messiah a priest for ever in his order.
John's Gethsemane.
Hebrews 5:7 speaks of loud cries and tears; Matthew 26:39 and Luke 22:44 tell of the agony in the garden.
The grain of wheat.
Paul uses the same picture for the resurrection of the body: what you sow does not come to life unless it dies (1 Corinthians 15:36).
outline: Opening
Ask: what am I keeping safe in the granary that God wants me to sow?
Point 1 · They sat down to eat
Jealousy, a pit, and twenty pieces of silver.
Point 2 · The LORD is among us
Trust that brings peace.
Point 3 · Loud cries and tears
The high priest who learned obedience.
Point 4 · Unless a grain of wheat falls
Glory through the Cross.
Take-home line
“unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains just a single grain”
live: Uproot one jealousy (Genesis 37:11)
Name before God one person you envy, and pray for their good today.
Pray for priests (Hebrews 5:1–2)
Pray by name for the priests of your parish and family, and thank one of them before Pesaha.
Let a grain fall (John 12:24)
Give up one comfort today for someone else's good, quietly and gladly.
We wish to see Jesus (John 12:21)
Bring one person who has been away to see Jesus at the Holy Week services.
fathers: St Caesarius of Arles (in substance)

Joseph was sold by his brothers, Christ by his disciple; Joseph was stripped of his robe, Christ of his garments; Joseph went down into the pit and was raised to rule Egypt, Christ went down into death and rose to rule heaven and earth.
St Augustine (in substance)
He himself was the grain that had to die and be multiplied: he died through the unbelief of some and was multiplied in the faith of the nations.
magis: Catechism 612
The cup of the new covenant, which Jesus anticipated at the Last Supper, he accepted from his Father in his agony in the garden, making himself obedient unto death.
Catechism 1544
Everything that the priesthood of the Old Covenant prefigured finds its fulfilment in Christ Jesus, the one mediator between God and men.
Catechism 2538–2539
Envy can lead to the worst crimes; it is a capital sin that the baptized must fight with goodwill.
Catechism 999
How do the dead rise? Paul answers with the seed: what you sow does not come to life unless it dies.
2027-03-23.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you were stripped of your garments and sold for silver like Joseph, and you offered prayers with loud cries and tears to the Father. Uproot the jealousy that divides our families, keep us faithful to one another, and make us a people among whom you are known to dwell. Teach us to follow you as the grain of wheat that falls into the earth, so that our lives may bear much fruit. Bless our priests, chosen from among us, and make them gentle with the wayward. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: The grain of wheat that fell into the earth and rose is given to us in the Holy Qurbana as the Bread of Life.
At the altar Christ, our high priest according to the order of Melchizedek, offers himself to the Father, and the priest chosen from among us lends him his hands and voice.

2027-03-24.title: Seventh Wednesday of the Great Fast · Wednesday of Hasha Week
2027-03-24.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: The new covenant sealed in blood
The Son of Man must be lifted up
2027-03-24.alt: Hasha Week (Holy Week), the last week of the Great Fast. Tomorrow is Pesaha: homes prepare the Pesaha appam and paal, and the parish prepares the one Qurbana of the Lord's Supper. In some traditions this day is called Spy Wednesday, recalling the bargain of Judas (Matthew 26:14–16).
2027-03-24.verse: And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.
theo: Joseph is now in an Egyptian prison, and two of Pharaoh's officers are thrown in with him: the chief cupbearer and the chief baker. One morning he finds them troubled and asks, “Why are your faces downcast today?” They have dreamed, and no one can explain the dreams. Joseph answers, “Do not interpretations belong to God? Please tell them to me.” The cupbearer saw a vine with three branches; it budded, blossomed and ripened, and “Pharaoh's cup was in my hand; and I took the grapes and pressed them into Pharaoh's cup, and placed the cup in Pharaoh's hand.” The baker saw three baskets of bread on his head, and birds eating from the top one. “The three branches are three days,” says Joseph, and within three days the cupbearer will be restored. Then the innocent prisoner adds a plea that goes to the heart: “But remember me when it is well with you; please do me the kindness to make mention of me to Pharaoh, and so get me out of this place.” “For in fact I was stolen out of the land of the Hebrews; and here also I have done nothing that they should have put me into the dungeon.” Everything happens as Joseph said, on the third day, and then comes the saddest line of the chapter: “Yet the chief cupbearer did not remember Joseph, but forgot him.” On the eve of Pesaha the Church sets before us a cup of wine, baskets of bread, an innocent man in chains, three days, and a plea to be remembered. On Friday a condemned man will say to Jesus, “Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23:42), and Jesus will not forget him. Tomorrow evening Jesus will take bread and the cup and say, “Do this in remembrance of me” (1 Corinthians 11:24). We are often the forgetful cupbearer; the Holy Qurbana is the place where we learn to remember, and where God remembers us. In Kerala homes this is the day of preparation: rice flour and coconut for the Pesaha appam, jaggery and coconut milk for the paal, and the little palm cross from Hosanna Sunday made ready.

In the second reading Joshua, old and near death, calls all Israel together for his farewell: “I am now old and well advanced in years; and you have seen all that the LORD your God has done to all these nations for your sake, for it is the LORD your God who has fought for you.” He asks one thing: “Therefore be very steadfast to observe and do all that is written in the book of the law of Moses, turning aside from it neither to the right nor to the left”, and “hold fast to the LORD your God, as you have done to this day.” His last word sums up the whole law: “Be very careful, therefore, to love the LORD your God.” Tomorrow Jesus will give his own farewell at the supper table, and his commandment will be the same, made new: love one another as I have loved you. The Epistle explains what Jesus will do with the cup. Christ “is the mediator of a new covenant”, and a covenant, like a will, takes effect through a death. “Hence not even the first covenant was inaugurated without blood.” Moses sprinkled the people and said, “This is the blood of the covenant that God has ordained for you.” Christ did not enter a sanctuary made by human hands, “but he entered into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf.” And he did not need to do it again and again: “he has appeared once for all at the end of the age to remove sin by the sacrifice of himself.” This is why the Church teaches that the Holy Qurbana is not a new or repeated sacrifice, but the one sacrifice of the Cross made present on our altars (Catechism 1366–1367). The letter ends with hope: Christ “will appear a second time, not to deal with sin, but to save those who are eagerly waiting for him.”

The Gospel lets us hear the Lord's heart on the eve of his Passion. “Now my soul is troubled.” John has no scene in the garden like the other Gospels; this is his Gethsemane. Jesus does not pretend to feel no fear. Yet he does not ask to be spared: “it is for this reason that I have come to this hour. Father, glorify your name.” A voice answers from heaven, “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again.” Some say it thundered; others say an angel spoke. Jesus tells them, “Now is the judgment of this world; now the ruler of this world will be driven out. And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.” John adds: “He said this to indicate the kind of death he was to die.” The Cross is a throne, a magnet, a light raised on a hill. The St Thomas Christians have kept for centuries a cross of their own, the Mar Thoma Sliva, carved without a figure, its arms blossoming, a dove descending upon it: the Cross seen already in the light of the Resurrection. Many still call this day Spy Wednesday, remembering that Judas went to the chief priests and asked, “What will you give me if I betray him to you?” (Matthew 26:15). Judas is not someone else's story. Each of us can sell the Lord for small things. But the One who will be lifted up draws all people to himself, even those who betrayed him, if they will only turn and look.
conn: Bread and wine in prison.
The cupbearer's cup and the baker's bread stand beside the innocent Joseph; the Fathers saw in them a faint sketch of the bread and the cup that Christ would give before his Passion.
Remember me.
Joseph pleads to be remembered (Genesis 40:14); the thief on the cross asks the same of Jesus (Luke 23:42); and Jesus says at the Supper, Do this in remembrance of me (Luke 22:19).
The third day.
The cupbearer is restored on the third day (Genesis 40:20); Hosea foresees that on the third day God will raise us up (Hosea 6:2); Christ was raised on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:4).
Farewell words.
Joshua's farewell (Joshua 23–24) and Jesus' farewell discourse at the Last Supper (John 13–17) both end in a call to love and hold fast.
The blood of the covenant.
Moses' words at Sinai (Exodus 24:8) are repeated in Hebrews 9:20 and fulfilled when Jesus says, This is my blood of the covenant (Matthew 26:28).
Lifted up.
Moses lifted up the bronze serpent (Numbers 21:8–9); Jesus says the Son of Man must be lifted up (John 3:14); Isaiah's servant shall be exalted and lifted up (Isaiah 52:13).
outline: Opening
Ask: whom have I forgotten, and do I believe that God remembers me?
Point 1 · Remember me
The cupbearer who forgot and the Lord who remembers.
Point 2 · Be very careful to love
Joshua's farewell and Jesus' commandment.
Point 3 · Once for all
The blood of the new covenant, made present at the altar.
Point 4 · When I am lifted up
The Cross that draws all people.
Take-home line
“And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.”
live: Prepare the Pesaha table
Prepare the Pesaha appam and paal together as a family, with the palm cross from Hosanna Sunday, and pray while you work.
Remember one forgotten person (Genesis 40:23)
Call or visit someone who once helped you and whom you have not thanked.
Look at the Cross (John 12:32)
Spend five quiet minutes before a crucifix or the Mar Thoma Sliva tonight.
Hold fast (Joshua 23:8)
Make a last good confession before Pesaha, if you have not yet done so.
fathers: St John Chrysostom (in substance)

Joseph asked the cupbearer to remember him, and was forgotten for two whole years. The thief asked Christ to remember him, and that very day he was in paradise. People forget those who did them good; Christ remembers even the sinner who turns to him at the last hour.
St Cyril of Jerusalem (in substance)
He stretched out his hands on the Cross to embrace the ends of the earth. Lifted up on Golgotha, the centre of the world, he draws all peoples to himself.
magis: Catechism 1366
The Eucharist is a sacrifice because it re-presents, makes present, the sacrifice of the Cross, and applies its fruit.
Catechism 1367
The sacrifice of Christ and the sacrifice of the Eucharist are one single sacrifice; only the manner of offering is different.
Catechism 662
Being lifted up on the Cross signifies and announces his lifting up by the Ascension into heaven.
Catechism 1085
The Paschal mystery of Christ cannot remain only in the past: it is made present in the liturgy.
2027-03-24.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, innocent one in chains, you did not forget the thief who begged to be remembered. Forgive us when we forget you and those who did us good. Mediator of the new covenant, you offered yourself once for all; make us worthy to stand at your altar tomorrow, where your one sacrifice is made present. Lifted up on the Cross, draw us and all people to yourself, and keep us faithful in love as Joshua taught his people. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: Joseph asked the cupbearer to remember him and was forgotten. At the Holy Qurbana Christ says, Do this in remembrance of me, and the Church never forgets: she makes his one sacrifice present until he comes.
The cup that the cupbearer placed in Pharaoh's hand was only wine; the cup the priest lifts at the altar is the blood of the new covenant.

2027-03-29.title: First Monday of Resurrection
2027-03-29.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
2027-03-29.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta). The first week of the Resurrection, traditionally the week of the newly baptised (neophytes): each day of this week shares the joy of Easter.
2027-03-29.verse: In a little while the world will no longer see me, but you will see me; because I live, you also will live.
theo: The first week after Easter was, in the ancient Church, the week of the newly baptised. Those who had come up from the font on the night of the Resurrection, dressed in white, came to the church every day to hear what had happened to them. The readings of this week still speak to them, and to every baptised Christian who wants to understand Easter from the inside. Isaiah speaks to a city that had been hated and abandoned: “Whereas you have been forsaken and hated, with no one passing through, I will make you majestic forever, a joy from age to age.” Then comes a promise that no city of stone could ever fulfil: “The sun shall no longer be your light by day, nor for brightness shall the moon give light to you by night; but the LORD will be your everlasting light, and your God will be your glory. Your sun shall no more go down, or your moon withdraw itself; for the LORD will be your everlasting light, and your days of mourning shall be ended.” The days of mourning ended on Easter morning. The Book of Revelation sees the same city at the end of time, needing no sun or moon, “for the glory of God is its light, and its lamp is the Lamb” (Revelation 21:23). The neophytes carried lit candles from the font; every Christian carries that light into an ordinary Monday.

On the day of Pentecost Peter stands up in Jerusalem and preaches the first Christian sermon. He reasons from the Psalms: David said that God would not abandon his Holy One to Hades or let him see corruption. But David died; “his tomb is with us to this day.” So David was speaking as a prophet, of the Messiah. “This Jesus God raised up, and of that all of us are witnesses. Being therefore exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this that you both see and hear.” The empty tomb of Jesus stands beside the full tomb of David: the difference between them is the whole Gospel. Peter speaks to his own people, the house of Israel, with the love of a brother, calling them to recognise their Messiah; the Church reads his words as a call to every one of us. Paul then shows how this new life is received: not by our works but by faith. “For what does the scripture say? ‘Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.’” And he quotes David's joy: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered; blessed is the one against whom the Lord will not reckon sin.” The newly baptised had just experienced exactly this: every sin washed away, not because they had earned it, but because they believed and were baptised into the Risen Christ. Faith is not opposed to good works; it is the root from which they grow. But the root comes first, and it is a gift.

In the Gospel Jesus speaks at the Last Supper, but every word looks towards Easter. “I will not leave you orphaned; I am coming to you. In a little while the world will no longer see me, but you will see me; because I live, you also will live.” The Resurrection is not only a fact about Jesus; it is the source of our life: because he lives, we live. He promises that the Father and he will come and make their home in whoever loves him and keeps his word: “Those who love me will keep my word, and my Father will love them, and we will come to them and make our home with them.” He promises the Advocate: “But the Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you everything, and remind you of all that I have said to you.” And he leaves his own gift: “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. I do not give to you as the world gives. Do not let your hearts be troubled, and do not let them be afraid.” This is the first word the Risen Lord will say when he comes through the locked doors on Easter evening: Peace be with you. The peace of Easter is not the absence of trouble but the presence of the Risen One. In the Syro-Malabar Qurbana, the priest gives the peace to the people before the anaphora, and the people pass it to one another: the peace of the Risen Lord, carried from the altar into our homes. In this first week of Easter, a family can make a simple practice of it: each evening, before sleep, say to one another, ‘The peace of the Lord be with you’.
conn: The everlasting light.
“The LORD will be your everlasting light” (Isaiah 60:19); the heavenly city has no need of sun or moon, “for the glory of God is its light, and its lamp is the Lamb” (Revelation 21:23).
David's tomb and the empty tomb.
Peter quotes Psalm 16:10, “you do not give me up to Sheol, or let your faithful one see the Pit”; Paul makes the same argument at Antioch (Acts 13:35–37).
Abraham's faith.
“And he believed the LORD; and the LORD reckoned it to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:6); Jesus “was handed over to death for our trespasses and was raised for our justification” (Romans 4:25).
The blessed forgiven.
Paul quotes Psalm 32:1–2. On Easter evening the Risen Lord gives the apostles the power to forgive sins (John 20:22–23).
Not orphans.
“Father of orphans and protector of widows is God in his holy habitation” (Psalm 68:5); Jesus promises, “I will not leave you orphaned” (John 14:18).
Peace be with you.
Jesus promises his peace (John 14:27) and gives it on Easter evening: “Peace be with you” (John 20:19).
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the promise of John 14 is kept: the Father and the Son come and make their home in those who receive the Body of Christ with love. Because he lives in us, we live.
The kiss of peace before the anaphora is the gift of the Risen Lord: not the peace the world gives, but his own, passed hand to hand from the altar.
outline: Opening
The neophytes in white, and the first Monday of a new life.
Point 1 · Your sun shall no more go down
Isaiah's everlasting light.
Point 2 · This Jesus God raised up
David's tomb and the empty tomb.
Point 3 · Reckoned as righteousness
Faith, forgiveness and the gift of grace.
Point 4 · Because I live, you also will live
The indwelling, the Advocate and the peace.
Closing image
A family saying ‘The peace of the Lord be with you’ before switching off the lights.
Take-home line
“Because I live, you also will live.”
live: Pass the peace at home (John 14:27)
Each evening this week, say to each other: The peace of the Lord be with you.
Thank God for forgiveness (Romans 4:7)
Make a good confession in this Easter week and thank God for the sins he no longer reckons.
Pray to the Advocate (John 14:26)
Before reading the Bible each day, say: Come, Holy Spirit, teach me and remind me.
Remember the newly baptised
Pray this week for those baptised at Easter, and for your own godchildren.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

He said, because I live, you also will live. He lives because he is God and because he has risen; we will live because he lives. His life is the cause of ours. He did not say ‘you live’, but ‘you will live’, because our resurrection is still to come in the body, yet already begun in faith and hope.
St Cyril of Jerusalem (in substance)

To the newly enlightened: you were led by the hand to the holy pool of divine Baptism, as Christ was carried from the Cross to the tomb. You went down into the water three times and came up again, and so in a figure you imitated the three days' burial of Christ. In the same moment you died and were born, and that saving water became both your tomb and your mother.
magis: Catechism 1987–1992
The grace of the Holy Spirit has the power to justify us, cleansing us from our sins; justification has been merited for us by the Passion of Christ and is conferred in Baptism.
Catechism 1996
Our justification comes from the grace of God; grace is the free and undeserved help God gives us to respond to his call.
Catechism 729
Jesus promises the coming of the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, who will teach and remind the disciples of all he said.
Catechism 260
The ultimate end of the whole divine economy is the entry of creatures into the perfect unity of the Trinity; even now we are called to be a dwelling for the Holy Trinity.
Catechism 1244
The newly baptised are dressed in white and given a lighted candle: Christ has enlightened them, and they are to walk as children of the light.
saints: This week
29 March–3 April: first week of the Resurrection. Friday 2 April: in the East Syriac tradition, the feast of all the saints (verify locally). Sunday 4 April: New Sunday (Puthu Njayar).
2027-03-29.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen and living, you promised not to leave us orphans, and you have come to us. Because you live, we live. Make your home in us with the Father, send us the Advocate to teach us and remind us of your words, and give us your peace, which the world cannot give. Keep the newly baptised in the light of their Baptism, and let us all walk as children of the light. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen. Alleluia!

2027-03-30.title: First Tuesday of Resurrection
2027-03-30.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
2027-03-30.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta). The first week of the Resurrection, the week of the newly baptised. The calendar notes the fuller passages: 1 Corinthians 15:1–19 and Luke 24:13–35.
2027-03-30.verse: Then beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted to them the things about himself in all the scriptures.
theo: “The spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me, because the LORD has anointed me; he has sent me to bring good news to the oppressed, to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and release to the prisoners.” These are the words Jesus read in the synagogue of Nazareth at the beginning of his ministry, saying, “Today this scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke 4:21). In Easter week they sound with new power. The Risen Christ is the Anointed One who has broken the greatest prison of all, the prison of death, and set its captives free. Isaiah continues: he comes “to provide for those who mourn in Zion, to give them a garland instead of ashes, the oil of gladness instead of mourning, the mantle of praise instead of a faint spirit.” On Ash Wednesday, at the start of the Great Fast, many of us received ashes; now the Lord gives us a garland. The newly baptised were anointed with the holy oil of chrism, the oil of gladness, and the prophet's next promise was for them and for us: “you shall be called priests of the LORD, you shall be named ministers of our God.” Every baptised Christian shares in the priesthood of Christ, offering his whole life with Christ to the Father at the Holy Qurbana. And the people of God become builders again: “They shall build up the ancient ruins, they shall raise up the former devastations; they shall repair the ruined cities.” Easter sends us to rebuild what sin has ruined, in our families, in our parishes, in our land.

Acts shows what happened when Peter finished his Pentecost sermon. “Now when they heard this, they were cut to the heart and said to Peter and to the other apostles, ‘Brothers, what should we do?’ Peter said to them, ‘Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ so that your sins may be forgiven; and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. For the promise is for you, for your children, and for all who are far away, everyone whom the Lord our God calls to him.’” About three thousand were baptised that day. Then Luke paints the first Christian community in four strokes: “They devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching and fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers.” Teaching, fellowship, the Eucharist, prayer: the four pillars of every Christian life and every parish. They shared their goods with anyone in need; “Day by day, as they spent much time together in the temple, they broke bread at home and ate their food with glad and generous hearts.” Paul then answers those who doubt the resurrection of the dead. If there is no resurrection, Christ has not been raised; “and if Christ has not been raised, then our proclamation has been in vain and your faith has been in vain.” “If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins.” “If for this life only we have hoped in Christ, we are of all people most to be pitied.” The Christian faith stands or falls with the bodily Resurrection of Jesus. It is not a beautiful symbol or a way of saying that his message lives on. It is a fact on which everything else rests, and it is the promise of our own resurrection in the body.

The Gospel is the walk to Emmaus. On the evening of the first day of the week, two disciples are walking away from Jerusalem, about seven miles, talking over everything that had happened. “While they were talking and discussing, Jesus himself came near and went with them, but their eyes were kept from recognizing him.” He asks what they are discussing, “They stood still, looking sad.” Cleopas tells the story of Jesus of Nazareth, a prophet mighty in deed and word, condemned and crucified, and then the saddest sentence in the Gospels: “But we had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel.” They even tell him about the women and the empty tomb, “but they did not see him.” Then the stranger speaks: “Oh, how foolish you are, and how slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have declared! Was it not necessary that the Messiah should suffer these things and then enter into his glory?” “Then beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted to them the things about himself in all the scriptures.” The full passage goes on: at the table he takes bread, blesses and breaks it, and their eyes are opened; they say, “Were not our hearts burning within us while he was talking to us on the road, while he was opening the scriptures to us?”, and they run back to Jerusalem. The shape of Emmaus is the shape of the Holy Qurbana: first the Word, in which Christ opens the Scriptures and our hearts burn; then the breaking of the bread, in which we recognise him; then the sending, as we go back to our brothers and sisters with the news. Our Qurbana does not begin with the bread but with the Word, and it does not end at the altar but on the road home.
conn: The anointed one.
Jesus reads Isaiah 61:1–2 at Nazareth and says, “Today this scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke 4:16–21).
Priests of the LORD.
“you shall be called priests of the LORD” (Isaiah 61:6); the baptised are “a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation” (1 Peter 2:9).
Cut to the heart.
On the day of Pentecost the hearers were cut to the heart (Acts 2:37); “I will remove from your body the heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 36:26).
The breaking of bread.

The first Christians devoted themselves to the breaking of bread (Acts 2:42); the Emmaus disciples recognised Jesus “in the breaking of the bread” (Luke 24:35); “The bread that we break, is it not a sharing in the body of Christ?” (1 Corinthians 10:16).
Firstfruits.
If Christ has not been raised our faith is futile (1 Corinthians 15:17); “But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the first fruits of those who have died” (1 Corinthians 15:20).
Moses and all the prophets.
The suffering and glory of the Messiah were foretold: the Servant of Isaiah 53, the psalm of the rejected stone (Psalm 118:22), and the sign of Jonah (Matthew 12:40).
altar: Every Holy Qurbana is an Emmaus. In the readings and the homily, the Risen Lord opens the Scriptures to us; in the breaking of the Holy Bread (the fraction), he makes himself known; and at the dismissal he sends us back on the road with burning hearts.
The first Christians devoted themselves to the breaking of bread; a parish that puts the Sunday Qurbana at the centre of its life is a parish built on the first pillar of the Church.
outline: Opening
Two disciples walking away from Jerusalem, and a stranger who joins them.
Point 1 · The spirit of the Lord is upon me
A garland instead of ashes; priests of the Lord.
Point 2 · Brothers, what should we do?
Repentance, Baptism, and the four pillars of the Church.
Point 3 · If Christ has not been raised
Everything rests on the Resurrection.
Point 4 · He opened the scriptures
Emmaus, the shape of the Qurbana.
Closing image
Two travellers running back in the dark, hearts burning, to tell the others.
Take-home line
“Were not our hearts burning within us?”
live: Read the Scriptures with him (Luke 24:27)
This week read one Old Testament passage about the Messiah (Isaiah 53 or Psalm 22) and ask Jesus to explain it to you.
Build up the ruins (Isaiah 61:4)
Repair one broken relationship in your family or neighbourhood this Easter week.
The four pillars (Acts 2:42)
Check your week: teaching, fellowship, the Qurbana, prayer. Strengthen the weakest one.
Walk with someone sad (Luke 24:15)
Visit or call someone who is going through a hard time, and simply walk with them.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

The Lord walked with them, and they did not know him; he was hidden from their eyes until the breaking of the bread. Learn where to find Christ: in the breaking of bread. Those who believe and receive him there recognise him. Do not think you are far from the Lord if you are among those who break this bread with faith.
St Gregory the Great (in substance)

The two disciples did not yet believe, yet they were speaking of him, and so he came to them. He showed himself outwardly as a stranger, because inwardly he was a stranger to their hearts. They invited him in as a guest, and in the breaking of bread they knew him. Practise hospitality, so that you may welcome Christ in the stranger.
magis: Catechism 1346–1347

The Eucharistic celebration has two great parts, the liturgy of the Word and the liturgy of the Eucharist; this is the same movement as the Paschal meal of the Risen Jesus with the disciples of Emmaus.
Catechism 1329
The ‘Breaking of Bread’ is one of the names of the Eucharist: by it the disciples recognised the Risen Christ.
Catechism 2624
In the first community of Jerusalem believers devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread and the prayers; this sequence is typical of the Church's prayer.
Catechism 651–655
The Resurrection confirms all that Christ did and taught; it is the principle and source of our own future resurrection.
Catechism 1268
The baptised share in the priesthood of Christ, in his prophetic and royal mission.
saints: Today
30 March: St John Climacus, abbot of Mount Sinai and author of ‘The Ladder of Divine Ascent’ (seventh century), remembered in the universal Church.
2027-03-30.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen companion on our road, you came near to the two disciples when their hope had died, and you opened the Scriptures until their hearts burned. Walk with us when we are sad and slow to believe. Open the Scriptures to us, make yourself known to us in the breaking of the Bread, and send us back to our brothers and sisters with the joyful news that you are alive. Make us one community, devoted to the teaching of the apostles, the fellowship, the breaking of bread and the prayers. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen. Alleluia!

2027-03-31.title: First Wednesday of Resurrection
2027-03-31.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: The faithful are strengthened through prayer
2027-03-31.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta). The first week of the Resurrection, the week of the newly baptised. The calendar notes the fuller passages: Ephesians 4:1–16 and John 15:1–25.
2027-03-31.verse: I am the vine, you are the branches. Those who abide in me and I in them bear much fruit, because apart from me you can do nothing.
theo: “I will greatly rejoice in the LORD, my whole being shall exult in my God; for he has clothed me with the garments of salvation, he has covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decks himself with a garland, and as a bride adorns herself with her jewels.” In Easter week these words were sung over the newly baptised, who had just put on white garments. Every Christian has been clothed by God: not with a robe we earned, but with Christ himself. “As many of you as were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ” (Galatians 3:27). Then Isaiah turns to Zion, the forsaken city, and speaks of a wedding. “You shall no more be termed Forsaken, and your land shall no more be termed Desolate; but you shall be called My Delight Is in Her, and your land Married; for the LORD delights in you.” “For as a young man marries a young woman, so shall your builder marry you, and as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you.” This is the language of the Easter Church. Christ the Bridegroom has given his life for his bride, the Church, and has risen to rejoice over her. The East Syriac liturgy loves this image: the Church is the bride betrothed to Christ, and the Holy Qurbana is the wedding feast. On Easter, God gives his people a new name: not Forsaken but My Delight. Every baptised person, however unworthy he feels, can hear the Risen Lord say to him: you are my delight.

In Acts, Peter and John have been arrested for healing a lame man in the name of Jesus and for preaching the Resurrection. They are threatened and released. They go back to their friends, and the whole community does not panic or complain; it prays. “When they heard it, they raised their voices together to God and said, ‘Sovereign Lord, who made the heaven and the earth, the sea, and everything in them’.” They read their situation in the light of Psalm 2: the rulers of the earth gathered against the Lord and his Anointed. And they do not ask for the threats to end, or for revenge. They ask for courage: “And now, Lord, look at their threats, and grant to your servants to speak your word with all boldness, while you stretch out your hand to heal, and signs and wonders are performed through the name of your holy servant Jesus.” The answer comes at once: “When they had prayed, the place in which they were gathered together was shaken; and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke the word of God with boldness.” Paul, writing from prison, shows the fruit of that Spirit in the life of the community: “I therefore, the prisoner in the Lord, beg you to lead a life worthy of the calling to which you have been called, with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love, making every effort to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.” And he names the sevenfold unity of the Church: “There is one body and one Spirit, just as you were called to the one hope of your calling, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is above all and through all and in all.” The persecuted Church is strong when she prays together and when she stays one.

The Gospel is the parable of the vine, spoken at the Last Supper over the cup of wine. “I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinegrower. He removes every branch in me that bears no fruit. Every branch that bears fruit he prunes to make it bear more fruit.” The key word is ‘abide’, repeated again and again. “Abide in me as I abide in you. Just as the branch cannot bear fruit by itself unless it abides in the vine, neither can you unless you abide in me.” “I am the vine, you are the branches. Those who abide in me and I in them bear much fruit, because apart from me you can do nothing.” The branch does not produce fruit by effort but by staying connected; the sap of the vine does the work. The Risen Christ is not only an example to imitate but a life to share. We abide in him through Baptism, by which we are grafted into the vine; through the Holy Qurbana, in which he says, “Those who eat my flesh and drink my blood abide in me, and I in them” (John 6:56); through his word remaining in us; and through keeping his commandments. “As the Father has loved me, so I have loved you; abide in my love.” The pruning is not punishment but care: the Father cuts back what is useless so that we may bear more fruit. Many a Christian has found that a time of loss or suffering became a time of greater fruitfulness. The vine of Kerala's ancient Christian community has been pruned many times in its long history, and it still bears fruit in vocations, in missionaries, in families of faith across the world, because it abides in the vine.
conn: Clothed with salvation.

“he has clothed me with the garments of salvation” (Isaiah 61:10); the baptised “have clothed yourselves with Christ” (Galatians 3:27); the saints in heaven wear robes made white in the blood of the Lamb (Revelation 7:14).
The bride and the Bridegroom.

“as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you” (Isaiah 62:5); “Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25); John sees the holy city “prepared as a bride adorned for her husband” (Revelation 21:2).
A new name.

Zion receives “a new name that the mouth of the LORD will give” (Isaiah 62:2); to the one who conquers the Risen Lord gives “a white stone, and on the white stone is written a new name” (Revelation 2:17).
The prayer of Psalm 2.
The community prays Psalm 2:1–2 (Acts 4:25–26); the same psalm says, “You are my son; today I have begotten you” (Psalm 2:7), which Paul applies to the Resurrection (Acts 13:33).
One body, one bread.
“Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread” (1 Corinthians 10:17); “that they may all be one” (John 17:21).
The vine of Israel.
Israel was the vine brought out of Egypt (Psalm 80:8); Isaiah sang of the vineyard that yielded wild grapes (Isaiah 5:1–7); Jesus is the true vine in whom the people of God bears fruit (John 15:1).
altar: The vine was spoken over the cup of the Last Supper. At every Holy Qurbana the fruit of the vine becomes the Blood of Christ, and those who drink it abide in him and he in them.
The one bread and one cup make us one body: the unity Paul begs us to keep is received at the altar before it is lived in the parish.
outline: Opening
A vine in a Kerala courtyard, its branches pruned and green again.
Point 1 · Clothed with salvation
My Delight Is in Her: the Bridegroom's joy over his people.
Point 2 · Grant us boldness
The persecuted Church prays and is filled with the Spirit.
Point 3 · One Lord, one faith, one baptism
Keeping the unity of the Spirit.
Point 4 · Abide in me
The vine, the branches and the pruning.
Closing image
A small room in Jerusalem shaking as a frightened community finishes its prayer.
Take-home line
“Apart from me you can do nothing.”
live: Abide (John 15:4)
Stay ten minutes before the Blessed Sacrament this week, or ten minutes in silence with the Gospel, simply abiding.
Pray for boldness (Acts 4:29)
When afraid to speak of your faith, pray the community's prayer: Lord, grant me to speak your word with boldness.
Bear with one another (Ephesians 4:2)
Choose one person in your family or parish who tests your patience, and bear with them in love this week.
Pray for persecuted Christians
Remember those who suffer for Christ today, and pray for them by name where you know of them.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

The branches are in the vine not so as to give anything to the vine, but so as to receive from it the life by which they live; the vine is in the branches to give them life, not to receive it. So it is good for the disciples to abide in Christ, but it adds nothing to him. Cut off, a branch can do nothing; it is fit either for the vine or for the fire.
St Ephrem the Syrian (in substance)

The Church is the bride whom the Son betrothed to himself on the Cross and adorned with his own Blood. Her wedding garment is the robe of glory she lost in Adam and received again in the water of Baptism. Let her rejoice, for her Bridegroom is risen and lives for ever.
magis: Catechism 787–789
From the beginning Jesus associated his disciples with his own life; the Church is communion with him, as the branches with the vine.
Catechism 796
The unity of Christ and the Church, head and members, is expressed by the image of bridegroom and bride.
Catechism 813–815
The Church is one: one Lord, one faith, one Baptism; her unity is kept by charity, the profession of one faith, common worship and apostolic succession.
Catechism 1108
The Holy Spirit unites the Church to the life of Christ, the vine, so that she may bear fruit.
Catechism 2636
The first Christian communities prayed intensely for one another; in persecution they asked for boldness to proclaim the Word.
saints: Today
31 March: St Benjamin, deacon and martyr in Persia (died about 424), a witness of the Church of the East who would not stop speaking of Christ.
2027-03-31.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, true vine, the Father has grafted us into you through Baptism and feeds us with your Body and Blood. Let us abide in you as you abide in us, and let your word remain in us. Prune from us what is useless, so that we may bear much fruit for the glory of the Father. Clothe us with the garments of salvation, keep your Church one in the bond of peace, and give us boldness to speak your word, as you gave it to the apostles when the house was shaken. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen. Alleluia!

quick: Hagar, a runaway slave, meets God by a spring and names him El-roi, the God who sees.
Israel keeps its oath to Gibeon, and the outsiders end up serving at the altar.
Present your bodies as a living sacrifice; Jesus is the living water and the light of the world.
2027-03-07.action: Thank by name one person who serves you unseen, and pay them justly.
2027-03-07.question: Where have I come from, where am I going, and whom have I failed to see?
catechism: The living sacrifice of the moral life.
Water, sign of the Holy Spirit.
I look at him and he looks at me.
kidsaint: Sts Perpetua and Felicity

They died for Jesus in Carthage, in North Africa, on 7 March 203. Perpetua was a young mother from a noble family; Felicity was a slave who gave birth to a baby girl in prison just before they died. In the world one was a lady and the other a servant, but in Jesus they were sisters, and they gave each other the kiss of peace before they died. Lesson: in God's family no one is less important than anyone else!
2027-03-07.special: Fifth Sunday of the Great Fast.
term: El-roi
A Hebrew name for God given by Hagar in Genesis 16:13, usually understood as “the God who sees” or “the God who sees me”. It reminds us that no suffering is hidden from God.

family.explain: Hagar was a servant girl. She was treated badly, so she ran away into the desert, all alone, with a baby on the way. But God found her beside a spring of water! He spoke kindly to her and promised to look after her and her baby. Hagar gave God a beautiful name: the God who sees me. God sees you too, always, wherever you are.
family.intention: We pray for women and children who are treated badly and feel that no one sees them.
family.ask: Ask: “Who works for us or helps us that we hardly ever notice? How can we thank them this week?”

illus: An illustration

A woman from Kottayam worked for eleven years as a housemaid in a Gulf city. In one house she was not allowed to go out, and she ate alone in the kitchen after everyone else. Every night she prayed with a small picture of the Sacred Heart hidden in her suitcase. Years later, back in Kerala, she told her parish prayer group: “I thought nobody in the world could see me. But I knew one thing. God saw me. That is how I lived.” When she finished, a young mother in the group went home and, for the first time, sat down to eat with the woman who cleaned her house.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you are the God who sees, the living water and the light of the world. See us now, and let us see you. Amen.
share: Hagar, where have you come from and where are you going? (Genesis 16:8). Where is my life heading this Lent?
We have sworn to them by the LORD; we must not touch them (Joshua 9:19). What promise have I failed to keep?
Present your bodies as a living sacrifice (Romans 12:1). What part of myself have I not yet offered to God?
Let anyone who is thirsty come to me (John 7:37). What am I thirsty for, and where am I looking for it?
pm.resp: Lord, give us living water.
interc: For the Church, that she may be a spring in the desert for all who are thirsty.
For domestic workers, migrants and all who are mistreated behind closed doors.
For husbands and wives, that they may keep their vows even when it costs.
For those preparing for Baptism this Easter, that they may receive the living water and the light.
For our parish, that we may love genuinely and serve the Lord with ardent spirit.
pm.close: Father, you saw Hagar in the desert and you sent your Son as living water and light. See all who suffer unseen, make us faithful to our word, and let our lives be a living sacrifice pleasing to you. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: Lot lingered, and God's mercy took him by the hand; his wife looked back and was lost.
Not one of God's promises failed; Paul asks us never to be a stumbling block, for the kingdom is not food and drink.
Jesus, the Good Shepherd, lays down his life freely, and will gather one flock.
2027-03-14.action: Make a definite break this week with the one thing you keep looking back at.
2027-03-14.question: What am I looking back at, and whom might my freedom cause to stumble?
catechism: The Church as sheepfold and flock.
kidsaint: St Matilda

She was a queen in Germany more than a thousand years ago, and she died on 14 March 968. She loved to help the poor and gave away so much that her own sons complained, and they even treated her unkindly. But Matilda forgave them, prayed for them, and they made peace again. Lesson: in a family, forgiveness is stronger than quarrels!
2027-03-14.special: Sixth Sunday of the Great Fast.
term: Stumbling block (scandal)

From the Greek skandalon, a trap or an obstacle on the road. In the Bible and in the Catechism, scandal means any word or deed that leads another person into sin. Paul asks Christians to give up even lawful things rather than cause a brother or sister to fall.

family.explain: Jesus says: I am the good shepherd. A good shepherd knows every one of his sheep by name and keeps them safe. When a wolf comes, a lazy helper runs away, but the good shepherd stays and protects the sheep, even if it costs his life. Jesus loves us like that. He gave his life for us on the Cross, and he rose again!
family.intention: We pray for our bishop and our parish priest, the shepherds of our Church.
family.ask: Ask: “How does Jesus our Shepherd take care of our family? Let each of us say one way.”

illus: An illustration

A man in a parish in Wayanad stopped drinking during the Great Fast every year, and every year started again on Easter Sunday afternoon with his friends. One Lent his teenage son came home late, smelling of beer, and said: you do it too, Pachan. The father did not shout. That night he told his son that he would not drink again, not for Lent but for good, and asked him to keep him to it. Years later, at the son's wedding, there was no liquor at the reception. When a relative complained, the son said only: my father gave it up so that I would not fall. This is my thanks to him.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, Good Shepherd, we hear your voice; gather us now as your one flock. Amen.
share: But he lingered (Genesis 19:16). Where am I lingering, knowing I should leave?
Not one of all the good promises that the LORD had made had failed (Joshua 21:45). Which of God's promises has he kept in my life?
Resolve never to put a stumbling block in the way of another (Romans 14:13). Is there anything in my life that might make someone else fall?
The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11). How is the Good Shepherd caring for me now?
pm.resp: Lord, Good Shepherd, lead us.
interc: For the Church, that she may be one flock under one shepherd.
For our bishops and priests, that they may lay down their lives for their people and never be hired hands.
For those who struggle with alcohol and other addictions, and for their families.
For those who linger at the door of conversion this Lent.
For unity among all the Churches of the St Thomas Christians.
pm.close: Father, you sent your Son as the Good Shepherd, who lays down his life and takes it up again. Take us by the hand when we linger, keep us faithful to your promises, make us careful of our brothers and sisters, and bring us with him through his Passion to the joy of his Resurrection. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: The scepter of Judah and the humble King on a donkey: the prophecies meet on the road to Jerusalem.
Jesus cleanses the house of prayer, heals the blind and the lame, and accepts the praise of children.
We are branches grafted onto a holy root; no room for pride, only gratitude.
2027-03-21.action: Keep the blessed palm in your prayer corner and gather the family for prayer each evening this week.
2027-03-21.question: Will the Hosanna I sing today still be on my lips on Friday?
catechism: The Jews are not collectively responsible for Jesus' death.
kidsaint: St Nicholas of Flüe

He was a Swiss farmer and the father of ten children, who died on 21 March 1487. Later in life, with his wife's agreement, he lived as a hermit and prayed for his country. When Switzerland was about to fall into civil war, the leaders asked his advice, and his words of peace kept the country together. Lesson: Jesus is the King of peace, and he wants us to be peacemakers too!
2027-03-21.special: Hosanna Sunday; the Week of the Passion begins.
term: Hosanna (Oshana)

A Hebrew cry meaning “Save us, we pray”, from Psalm 118. The crowds shouted it when Jesus entered Jerusalem; the Church sings it in the Holy Qurbana, and the Sunday before Easter takes its name from it.

family.explain: Jesus rode into Jerusalem on a little donkey. The people were so happy that they put their coats on the road and waved branches from the trees. They shouted: “Hosanna! Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord!” Today we wave our palm leaves to welcome Jesus too. He is a King, but a gentle King who comes on a donkey, not on a war horse.
